# PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?

Sachin Konan  Jonathan Liu  Zhuang Liu  
Princeton University

[Website](https://sachinkonan.github.io/PaperScorer.html)  
[Code](https://github.com/zlab-princeton/PaperScorer)  ![[Uncaptioned
image]](2610.31791v1/figures/logos/hf.png) [Hugging
Face](https://huggingface.co/collections/zlab-princeton/paperscorer)

![Refer to caption](2610.31791v1/teaser_flow.png)

(a) PaperScorer predicts a paper’s decision from its text or visual
view.

(b) Two anonymized corpora.

(c) PaperScorer is an accurate decision predictor.

Figure 1: (a) PaperScorer is a family of models trained to predict a
paper’s accept/reject decision from either a pure text or a visual view
of the paper. (b) For training and evaluation, we built two fully
anonymized datasets, sourced from OpenReview and arXiv and labeled with
accept/reject decisions. (c) Across training recipes, we find
fine-tuning on our large-scale corpora enables PaperScorer to exceed
frontier models (GPT/Gemini), specifically on highly rated papers.

Abstract

- Automated research is largely evaluated by benchmark performance, but
  the value of research rarely reduces to a single score. Humans judge a
  work’s holistic contribution through peer review, which is hard to
  model because it is noisy and depends on many factors. However, what
  if, given only the paper, we could predict its peer-review decision
  directly? We introduce PaperScorer, a family of models that predict a
  paper’s accept or reject decision from its extracted text or page
  screenshots, training only on the decision after removing author
  identity and formatting shortcuts. Vision models are the most
  predictive (68% accuracy on ICLR papers and 77% on ML papers from
  arXiv), beating text-only and frontier reasoning models. Unlike plain
  text, page images retain figures, layout, and presentation. This
  signal is robust, surviving smaller models and even compressing the
  whole paper into a single image. But accurate predictions are not
  evenly spread. PaperScorer is strongest on the lowest and highest
  rated papers, while papers rated in the middle stay unpredictable for
  our models and frontier systems alike. Additionally, its confidence is
  calibrated, so its most confident predictions are also its most
  accurate. Overall, PaperScorer shows how much of the decision a paper
  carries on its own, marking a first step toward AI-driven research
  evaluation.

## Section 1 Introduction

Increasingly capable large language model (LLM) agents are beginning to
automate research end to end, proposing ideas, running experiments, and
interpreting the results to recursively self-improve ([Lu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28); [Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib46); [Si et al.,
2026](#bib.bib37); [Favaro and Clark, 2026](#bib.bib12)). This loop
needs a way to judge whether a result is good, and the standard judge is
a benchmark. Optimizing benchmarks has driven much of the field’s
progress, from ImageNet in computer vision ([Deng et al.,
2009](#bib.bib11)) to MuJoCo in reinforcement learning ([Todorov et al.,
2012](#bib.bib41)). Yet many contributions, such as findings or
interpretability work, have no benchmark, and even where they exist,
researchers disagree about which ones matter. This necessitates peer
review.

However, peer review is noisy and poorly understood. A paper is
typically judged by three or four reviewers and a meta-reviewer, whose
assessments are combined into a final accept or reject decision
([Yacoby, 2022](#bib.bib45)). In the NeurIPS ’14 and ’21 consistency
experiments, roughly half of papers accepted by one committee would not
have been accepted by the other ([Beygelzimer et al., 2021](#bib.bib5)).
AI tools now add to this complexity ([Biswas et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)),
as up to 17% of reviews were materially edited by LLMs ([Liang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib26)), and LLM-generated feedback led 27% of treated
reviewers to revise their reviews ([Thakkar et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)).
A final decision therefore mixes paper signal with noise from reviewer
assignment, interpretation, aggregation, and now the AI tools involved.
Before automated systems can judge research the way peer review does, we
need to know how much of the decision the paper itself determines. This
motivates a simple question:

_From paper content alone, how predictable is the final decision?_

Measuring this signal requires more than fitting accept/reject labels.
Without careful controls, a predictor can rely on shortcut signals
rather than paper content ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib52)).
Camera-ready formatting, author-identifying text, source-specific
artifacts, and the natural majority-reject rate can all leak the label
([Jin et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)). Even after removing shortcuts, final
decisions remain noisy, so a useful model should report uncertainty,
separating confident cases from papers whose outcomes are not
predictable from content alone.

We introduce PaperScorer, a family of models that predicts binary
acceptance decisions from anonymized papers. PaperScorer is trained on
final outcomes rather than intermediate reviews or ratings, using
anonymized datasets of machine learning (ML) papers. To test whether
extracted text is sufficient, we compare two representations of each
paper, markdown for text models and screenshots of each page for vision
models. The text representation contains all text, including formulas
and tables, but excludes figures, while vision preserves the full
document. Our datasets contain fully anonymized papers from ICLR, which
are openly hosted and shared on OpenReview, and from ML conferences on
arXiv, all from ’20–’26 and balanced 50/50 accept/reject to avoid a
majority-reject shortcut.

Our main empirical result is that paper content contains recoverable
decision signal, but this signal is limited. Our top vision model,
PaperScorer-Vision, achieves 68% accuracy on ICLR, improving over the
best frontier baseline by 2.7%. On arXiv, arXiv-trained
PaperScorer-Vision achieves 77% accuracy, improving over frontier
baselines by 9.0%. Beyond binary decisions, PaperScorer emits a
continuous acceptance estimate. This score ranks accepted above rejected
papers across thresholds, and on ICLR, it aligns with reviewer ratings
better than reviewer-trained baselines. After calibration on validation
data, confidence matches accuracy on our test datasets, so at $`X\%`$
confidence, accuracy is about $`X\%`$.

Our experiments isolate several factors underlying performance. First,
PaperScorer achieves significantly higher accuracy with vision than with
text on both datasets. Vision enables analysis of figures, layout, and
full-document presentation, signal that our text extraction discards.
Second, predictability is concentrated at the extremes of reviewer
rating, but not symmetrically. Frontier models reliably flag only the
lowest-rated papers, whereas PaperScorer is accurate on both low and
high-rated papers. Across all evaluated models, however, accuracy
remains near chance on papers with intermediate reviewer ratings, so for
these papers the document alone gives our models little to go on. Third,
performance improves with data scale but is largely invariant to model
size or input resolution. A 3B model performs similarly to a 7B model,
and compressing the whole paper into a single image only marginally
degrades performance.

In summary, PaperScorer is the strongest paper decision predictor in our
study, because a large, carefully controlled dataset lets
straightforward supervised fine-tuning deliver higher accuracy and
calibrated confidence, concentrated on the clear accepts and rejects.
This matters because automated research makes research faster to iterate
on, so submission volumes ([Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib50)) and reviewer
burden ([Adam, 2025](#bib.bib2)) rise, while benchmark scores tell only
part of a contribution’s story, which means evaluation must scale in a
way that reflects human judgment. At only 7B parameters, PaperScorer is
a first step that measures how much of the human decision the paper
alone carries, shows through calibration when to trust that estimate,
and already plugs into agentic reviewing and literature search
([Appendix
K](#A11 "Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

## Section 2 Problem Formulation

We study content-only paper acceptance prediction. Let $`\mathcal{X}`$
denote the space of observed paper artifacts and $`\mathcal{Z}=\{0,1\}`$
the final binary decision, with $`z=1`$ for acceptance and $`z=0`$ for
rejection. Our goal is to learn a predictor $`f_{\theta}(x)`$ that
returns, from the paper artifact alone, both a hard decision and a score
whose higher values indicate a higher predicted probability of
acceptance.

Peer review’s decision process. We view peer review as a latent chain
where $`X_{0}`$ is the initial submission, $`Y_{1}`$ the initial
reviews, $`Y_{2}`$ the rebuttal process, $`X_{\mathrm{reb}}`$ the
revised paper, $`R`$ the revised review after rebuttal, $`Y_{3}`$ the
meta-review, and $`Z`$ the final decision.

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
X_{0}\rightarrow Y_{1}\rightarrow Y_{2}\rightarrow X_{\mathrm{reb}}\rightarrow R\rightarrow Y_{3}\rightarrow Z
``` |  |

Because public anonymous artifacts are most consistently available after
rebuttal ([Appendix
B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Data Provenance and Ensuring Anonymity ‣ Appendix B Data Curation Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
documents year-over-year availability), our practical task is
$`p(Z\mid X_{\mathrm{reb}})`$ rather than $`p(Z\mid X_{0})`$. In
contrast with prior work ([Gao et al., 2024](#bib.bib13); [Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib56)), reviews, ratings, and meta-reviews are *not
regressed on*.

Prediction target. We frame this as a text-generation problem with a
decision-only target, so prompting, SFT, and RL can all be studied under
the same format.

|     |                                                                    |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       f_{\theta}(x)\rightarrow\boxed{\texttt{Accept}\mid\texttt{Reject}}
       ```                                                                 |     |

When token probabilities are available, we also compute an acceptance
score $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}(x)`$ by normalizing the probabilities
assigned to the two decision tokens. The target dataset is therefore a
collection $`\mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},z_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}`$ of paper-decision
pairs, where $`x_{i}`$ is derived from paper content alone and $`z_{i}`$
is the final conference decision.

Estimated Bayesian ceiling. As the NeurIPS ’14 / ’21 consistency
experiments ([Beygelzimer et al., 2021](#bib.bib5)) show, the decision
carries some amount of randomness. To get a rough sense of where the
ceiling on accuracy lies given this noise, we fit a Beta-Bernoulli model
loosely to this single historical experiment. Let $`p_{i}\in[0,1]`$
denote the latent acceptance probability of paper $`i`$, with committee
decisions drawn from independent Bernoulli distributions, implying the
following values.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[p]=0.26,\qquad\mathbb{E}[2p(1-p)]=0.23,\qquad\mathbb{E}[p^{2}]=\frac{0.52-0.23}{2}=0.145.
``` |  |

Matching these moments gives $`p\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)`$ with
$`(\alpha,\beta)\approx(0.39,1.10)`$. Under this fitted model, the
Bayes-optimal accuracy is approximately 83.3% under the original
acceptance distribution and 80.2% on a balanced accept/reject
evaluation. We use 80.2% only as a soft reference point, not a hard
limit, since this estimate is loose and inherits the assumptions of one
historical experiment. Full derivation is in [Appendix
A](#A1 "Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?").

## Section 3 PaperScorer: Dataset and Methods

This section describes the balanced ICLR and source-derived arXiv
corpora with paired markdown and page screenshots, and the training
recipes behind PaperScorer.

### 3.1 Datasets

PaperScorer uses two balanced, anonymous accept/reject sources, both
split 85/5/10 across train, validation, and test, and we evaluate on the
most recent years of each test split. ICLR contains 25K submissions from
OpenReview, evaluated on ’25–’26. arXiv contains LaTeX-source-derived
proceedings papers, evaluated on ’24–’26 to include biannual venues like
ECCV. arXiv training uses a large 83K set (arXiv) and a smaller 25K set
proportional to ICLR (arXiv-m). All datasets are balanced 50/50, and
[Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In 3.1 Datasets ‣ Section 3 PaperScorer: Dataset and Methods ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
shows examples from both.

![Refer to caption](2610.31791v1/dataset_panel_mosaic.png)

Figure 2: Dataset mosaic. Screenshots of pages from ICLR and arXiv. ICLR
examples use latest-rebuttal OpenReview PDFs, while arXiv examples are
derived from LaTeX source, recompiled with venue-specific anonymization
macros. Each example tiles multiple pages for visualization; in
practice, PaperScorer-Vision processes individual pages. Notably, ICLR
papers can contain rebuttal-era revisions (colored text), whereas
source-rendered arXiv papers do not.

A paper-decision dataset is useful only if the model sees the same
evidence that a final decision maker could have seen. We therefore
require three properties before a paper enters the corpus:

1.  1.
    Anonymity. The exported artifact should not reveal authors,
    affiliations, acknowledgments, source repositories, or camera-ready
    status that would leak the final review outcome to the model.
2.  2.
    Main-conference scope. Papers must be full main-conference
    submissions, excluding workshops, short papers, industry tracks,
    withdrawn records, and other items outside the target decision
    process.
3.  3.
    Consistent processing of accepts and rejects. Accept and reject
    artifacts should differ through natural paper content, not through
    formatting shortcuts, rendering, or availability cues.

Data sourcing. We build ICLR from OpenReview because ICLR releases both
accepted and rejected submissions with review metadata. The challenge is
obtaining the anonymized artifact rather than a post-review PDF. Across
six recent years, latest-rebuttal PDFs give the best availability for
anonymous artifacts ([Appendix
B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Data Provenance and Ensuring Anonymity ‣ Appendix B Data Curation Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
although they can contain rebuttal-era revisions in the artifact itself.
We therefore use ICLR ’20–’23, ’25, and ’26 and exclude ICLR ’24, where
accepts are only camera-ready.

Figure 3: Dataset coverage. We summarize the balanced PaperScorer pools
by ICLR year and arXiv venue after anonymous recompilation and
filtering. ICLR coverage leans toward later years, while arXiv coverage
is largest for NeurIPS, CVPR, and ACL-style NLP venues, with smaller
balanced slices from other ML conferences.

ICLR is only one machine-learning venue, so we also build a LaTeX-source
derived arXiv corpus for broader training and evaluation. arXiv does not
provide reject labels, but title matches to conference proceedings
provide high-precision accepted papers ([Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib50)). We therefore define an *implied reject* as a
LaTeX-compiling paper that uses a covered venue template, satisfies the
main-conference filters, and does not appear in that venue’s
proceedings. This gives a noisier but more diverse source whose accept
class is high fidelity and whose reject class tests whether the learned
decision boundary survives weak negative labels.

We use arXiv as a testbed for two transfer questions. First, within
arXiv, we ask whether diverse supervision improves classification on
held-out arXiv papers, paying particular attention to accept recall
because accepted papers have the strongest provenance. Second, across
sources, we compare arXiv-trained models on the high-fidelity ICLR set
and ICLR-trained models on arXiv. This isolates whether diversity
improves generalization or whether clean same-source labels remain more
valuable than a larger weakly labeled pool.

Data filtering and normalization. ICLR is primarily filtered by year and
artifact availability, then balanced within OpenReview year. arXiv
requires more reconstruction. Starting from 434,579 ML arXiv papers, we
pull 434,443 LaTeX source tarballs in bulk from arXiv’s requester-pays
S3 feed and extract their .tex contents with NeMo Curator’s
ArxivIterator/ArxivExtractor ([NVIDIA, 2024](#bib.bib33)). We then
detect venue style files, compile anonymous review-mode PDFs, and remove
residual identifiers. We drop non-main-conference, workshop, withdrawn,
industry-track, and short-format papers. For arXiv, we additionally
require a successful anonymous render, a references section, and between
six and 30 main content pages to ensure consistency across papers. Full
pipeline details for both sources are documented in [Appendix
B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Our Data Pipeline ‣ Appendix B Data Curation Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?").

The coverage plot in
[Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In 3.1 Datasets ‣ Section 3 PaperScorer: Dataset and Methods ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
reflects this sampling choice. ICLR starts with 40K ICLR submissions and
subsamples rejects to 25K while keeping the annual distribution. For
arXiv, submission year is more nebulous: implied rejects have upload
dates, while proceedings-matched accepts have conference years and
post-review uploads. We therefore do not year-balance arXiv, and instead
subsample 101,659 filtered papers to an 83,656 balanced set that keeps
the starting venue distribution.

Both sources pass through the same MinerU ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib43)) normalization before export. We remove headers,
line-numbering asides, author-identifying spans, and all content in and
after the references. Text models receive markdown with excluded regions
omitted, while vision models receive page screenshots with the same
regions whitened. Text inputs use the full markdown up to a pre-defined
$`24{,}480`$ max context length, while for vision, each page is rendered
and downscaled to at most $`1{,}003{,}520`$ pixels
($`1280{\times}28^{2}`$), roughly $`1{,}240`$ vision tokens. A typical
paper runs about ten pages (median $`10`$, up to $`33`$), so the vision
input averages roughly $`12{,}420`$ tokens, about half the max context
length. Accepted papers still contain more content, figures, and
citations after cleanup, reflecting differences in content rather than
artifact mismatches.

|                |             |       |              |       |
|----------------|-------------|-------|--------------|-------|
|                | ICLR (test) |       | arXiv (test) |       |
| Train Setting  | Vision      | Text  | Vision       | Text  |
| Natural train  | -9.2        | -34.5 | -43.0        | -49.8 |
| + val. thresh. | -6.0        | +27.9 | -10.8        | +8.7  |
| Balanced train | +1.8        | -6.6  | -3.2         | -1.6  |

Table 1: Training-prior bias. Accept$`-`$reject recall gap after each
prior/threshold rule; lower absolute value is better.

Why balanced training and evaluation? Conference decisions are naturally
imbalanced, so raw accuracy can reward a predictor that mostly rejects
papers. Therefore, we use a balanced test set, whereby accuracy equally
weights accept and reject recall. This still supports natural-rate
interpretation: for samples drawn from the same curated domain,
class-conditional recalls from a balanced test can be reweighted by the
known accept prior. In [Appendix
F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Evaluation and Training Prior Investigation ‣ Appendix F Training Variations ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"),
this predicts natural-rate accuracy to within a few percent on
ICLR/arXiv.

The training prior is a separate choice. Natural-rate training matches
the conference base rate, but the native decision rule then predicts
rejection too often, since rejects are the majority class.
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.1 Datasets ‣ Section 3 PaperScorer: Dataset and Methods ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
summarizes this as the gap between accept and reject recall.
Natural-rate ICLR and arXiv models predict rejection far more often than
acceptance under their native threshold, and tuning the threshold on
validation data can shift it too far the other way. Balanced-trained
models are closer to zero, so we use balanced training for the headline
PaperScorer models. This removes the excess rejection predictions
without per-dataset threshold tuning.

### 3.2 Methods

Chosen models. We use Qwen2.5 text and Qwen2.5-VL vision backbones
([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib48); [Bai et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)) because
our original deployment target was ICLR, and Qwen2.5 is the latest Qwen
generation that plausibly predates public ICLR ’25 decisions (text in
December ’24, VL on January 26, ’25). This makes ICLR a clean deployment
setting by the same cutoff logic, while later Qwen3/3.5 models are more
likely to have seen those results; arXiv was added later and did not
drive backbone selection. We also retrain a Qwen3 text backbone on ICLR
and find that swapping the base model moves accuracy little ([Appendix
E](#A5 "Appendix E Backbone Choice: Qwen2.5 vs. Qwen3 ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

Our main comparison is against DeepReview-7B/14B ([Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib56)) (trained through ICLR ’24), Gemini-3.1-Pro (January
’25 cutoff), and GPT-5.5 (December ’25 cutoff) reasoning baselines.
GPT-5.5’s cutoff postdates the public release of ICLR ’25 decisions, so
we probe it for memorization directly ([Appendix
D](#A4 "Appendix D Do Frontier Models Memorize the Test Decisions? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
It recognizes many of our test papers, but the decisions it claims to
recall are not reliable. Once its accept bias is accounted for, they are
at chance. It also cannot regenerate abstracts from titles (ROUGE-L
([Lin, 2004](#bib.bib27)) at noise level), and its accuracy on the
papers it recognizes matches its accuracy on those it does not,
including on ICLR ’25. These probes provide no clear evidence that
recalled acceptance decisions explain its baseline performance.

We additionally compare against Jev ([TypeSafe AI, 2026](#bib.bib42)), a
much cheaper model claimed to be well calibrated. It returns an
acceptance probability from text, so we give it the same input as
PaperScorer-Text and compare calibration in
[Section 5](#S5 "Section 5 Where does this signal lie? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?").

Baseline Prompting. For main results, DeepReview runs in its native
Standard Mode with four simulated reviewers, self-verification, and a
meta-review decision. Gemini/GPT baselines use one venue-generic
AI-Scientist-style prompt ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Yamada et
al., 2025](#bib.bib46)) that requests a 1–10 rating and an Accept/Reject
decision. Mini and large frontier variants run at high reasoning effort.
The generated decision is the default hard label, and the rating is a
ranking score, not a probability. Qwen rows use the answer-only
supervised fine-tuning (SFT) prompt or the reasoning
reinforcement-learning (RL) prompt ([Appendix
H.1](#A8.SS1 "H.1 Prompts ‣ Appendix H Prompting and Extended Experiments ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

We also evaluate frontier coding-agent harnesses with the same
rating-plus-decision task. Each Codex or Claude Code run receives an
isolated paper workspace with stripped markdown, page screenshots,
instructions, and a schema validator that enforces a well-formed
PREDICTIONS.json; we log the full trajectory in session.jsonl. Agents
run at the same high reasoning effort, inspect text and images
selectively, and stay siloed without internet (prompt and layout in
[Appendix
K.3](#A11.SS3 "K.3 Agentic Reviewer Prompts ‣ Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

Baseline Correction Measures. Under the base prompt, several models
strongly favor one decision class. We also tested more critical prompt
variants, but bringing predicted acceptance rates closer to 50% did not
reliably improve accuracy. We therefore retain the base prompt, the same
one used to start SFT/RL training, for the main comparisons. These base
prompts and their critical variants are defined in [Appendix
H.3](#A8.SS3 "H.3 Correcting Model Biases with Prompting ‣ Appendix H Prompting and Extended Experiments ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?").

For each baseline, we also tune a threshold on its score using a small
held-out sample of papers, and use the thresholded score as the hard
label when it improves accuracy. Out-of-the-box thresholds are skewed:
under its default threshold, GPT predicts rejection much more often than
acceptance, and Gemini leans the same way, though less strongly. Yet
both still show relatively high AUC, suggesting the predicted rating is
well-ordered while the chosen decision threshold is biased. Calibrating
the threshold generally helps baseline numbers, in agreement with the
findings of [Lu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib28).

SFT. Supervised fine-tuning is our primary method for studying data
representation, training distribution, scaling, and calibration. We
fine-tune Qwen2.5 text models at 3B, 7B, and 14B scale, and Qwen2.5-VL
models at 3B and 7B scale, using LLaMA-Factory ([Zheng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib55)). Let $`P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$ denote the model’s
next-token distribution at the decision token for paper $`x`$. In the
Qwen2.5 vocabulary, Accept and Reject are individual tokens, so we read
off the probability of each and normalize over the two:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{\mathrm{accept}}=\frac{P_{\theta}(\texttt{Accept}\mid x)}{P_{\theta}(\texttt{Accept}\mid x)+P_{\theta}(\texttt{Reject}\mid x)}.
``` |  |

After SFT, almost all decision mass lies on these two tokens (validated
across all models), so $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ behaves as a usable
binary accept probability. Full training settings are documented in
[Appendix
I.1](#A9.SS1 "I.1 SFT ‣ Appendix I SFT and RL Method Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?").
The SFT sweeps vary training source and scale, class prior, text versus
screenshot inputs, mixed text+vision inputs, and suffixes such as
handcrafted paper statistics or generated reviews ([Appendix
F.2](#A6.SS2 "F.2 Ablating Training Distribution and Paper Representation ‣ Appendix F Training Variations ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

RL. For reinforcement-learning variants, we fine-tune the policy with
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16)) using SkyRL ([Cao et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)) on the
same paper-only accept/reject task. The policy uses the reasoning
prompt, samples a group of completions for each paper, and updates using
within-group relative rewards rather than a learned reward model, so the
model can reason before its final label. We score each completion $`y`$
for paper $`x`$ with:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r(y,x)=0.8\cdot\mathbf{1}\!\left[d(y)=d^{\star}(x)\right]+0.2\cdot\mathbf{1}\!\left[\textsc{format}(y)\right],
``` |  |

where $`d(y)`$ extracts the boxed Accept/Reject decision with keyword
fallback, $`d^{\star}(x)`$ is the ground-truth decision, and
$`\textsc{format}(y)`$ checks that the completion has the required
\<think\>…\</think\> block followed by
\<answer\>\boxed{Accept\|Reject}\</answer\>. The format term matters
early in training, when many completions skip the boxed answer (details
in [Appendix
I.2](#A9.SS2 "I.2 RL ‣ Appendix I SFT and RL Method Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

## Section 4 Results

We first define our metrics
([Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Evaluation Metrics ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
then set a simple paper features baseline
([Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 A Simple Paper Features Baseline ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
and finally report main results against prompting and coding-agent
baselines
([Section 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

### 4.1 Evaluation Metrics

Each paper has a true decision $`z\in\mathcal{Z}`$, and each system
produces a hard prediction $`\hat{z}\in\mathcal{Z}`$ and an accept score
$`s\in[0,1]`$, where higher means more likely to be accepted. AUC
evaluates each system’s ranking without requiring its scores to
represent calibrated probabilities. For PaperScorer, $`s`$ is the accept
probability $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$, while for frontier models $`s`$ is
a normalized 1–10 rating.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Metric | Definition and role in evaluation |
| Primary metrics |  |
|  ^($`\star`$)Accuracy (Acc) |  Fraction of papers whose predicted decision matches the truth. On our balanced 50/50 test set, accepts and rejects count equally, so always-reject scores only $`50\%`$. |
|  ^($`\star`$)Area under the ROC curve (AUC) |  The model produces a score $`s`$, and across thresholds we plot the fraction of accepts called accept ($`y`$) against the fraction of rejects called accept ($`x`$); AUC is the area under this curve, the chance a random accept outscores a random reject. |
| Secondary diagnostics |  |
|  ^($`\diamond`$)Accept / reject recall ($`R_{A}`$, $`R_{R}`$) |  Model’s ability to recall all instances of each binary label. Shows whether errors lean toward accepts or rejects. |
|  ^($`\diamond`$)Predicted acceptance rate ($`p_{A}`$) |  Fraction of all papers the model calls accept. Near $`50\%`$ indicates that the model does not have an inherent bias toward the accept or reject class. |
|  ^($`\diamond`$)Rating correlation ($`\rho_{R}`$) |  Spearman correlation between the accept score $`s`$ and each paper’s average reviewer rating, measuring alignment with human judgments. |
|  ^($`\diamond`$)Expected calibration error (ECE) |  Average gap between confidence and accuracy across confidence bins on the balanced test. Low ECE means $`X\%`$-confidence predictions are right about $`X\%`$ of the time. |

Table 2: Evaluation diagnostics. Primary metrics (^($`\star`$)) steer
training and data decisions. Secondary diagnostics (^($`\diamond`$))
drive behavioral analysis. An ideal predictor is accurate (Acc), ranks
accepts above rejects (AUC), and is well calibrated.

When studying PaperScorer reliability, we ask whether confidence tracks
realized accuracy after post-hoc calibration. The decision confidence is
$`c=p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ for an Accept prediction and
$`c=1-p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ for a Reject prediction. We bin papers by
$`c`$, such that in each bin $`B_{m}`$, $`\mathrm{Acc}(B_{m})`$ is the
fraction of correct predictions and $`\mathrm{Conf}(B_{m})`$ is the
average confidence. ECE is the weighted gap
$`|\mathrm{Acc}(B_{m})-\mathrm{Conf}(B_{m})|`$ on the balanced test;
[Section 5](#S5 "Section 5 Where does this signal lie? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
also checks the acceptance probability at real acceptance rates.
Frontier ratings are 1–10 review-style scores, not accept/reject
probabilities, so we report calibration only for PaperScorer and Jev.

Our primary metrics ask whether a system both makes the right binary
decision and ranks accepted papers above rejected papers. The goal is to
design a predictor that makes human-like decisions while producing a
score that orders papers the way peer review does. Accuracy tests
whether predictions match final decisions without hiding accept/reject
collapse, while AUC tests whether accepted papers receive higher scores
than rejected papers independent of a fixed threshold. This matters
because the same model may be used on conferences or years outside its
training distribution, where post-hoc threshold tuning may not be
available. Secondary diagnostics separate class bias from rating
alignment and calibration.

### 4.2 A Simple Paper Features Baseline

Before training any large model, we ask how much of the accept/reject
decision is recoverable from simple, hand-crafted features. We fit two
full-data logistic-regression models, one on ICLR and one on arXiv,
using paper features such as length, references, math notation, topic
terms, and rhetorical counts. The models exclude source identifiers,
venue labels, ratings, citations, author names, and body-page counts,
since page metadata is not comparable between the ICLR and arXiv text
exports. These simple models reach 61.1% accuracy on ICLR and 62.5% on
arXiv. Their coefficients reveal which readily measured paper features
are associated with acceptance.
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.2 A Simple Paper Features Baseline ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
shows that accept features generally have to do with paper length,
references, and figures, while reject features are more lexical (full
inventory in [Appendix
C](#A3 "Appendix C Simple Feature Analysis ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

Baseline performance. We compare base Qwen instruct models, mini and
large frontier Gemini/GPT reasoning models, decision models, coding
agents, and DeepReview. Untuned Qwen2.5 predicts Accept for 97–99% of
papers ([Appendix
H.3](#A8.SS3 "H.3 Correcting Model Biases with Prompting ‣ Appendix H Prompting and Extended Experiments ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
Smaller high-reasoning models are also skewed natively, with
Gemini-3-Flash accepting almost every paper and GPT-5.4-Mini rejecting
almost every paper. Large frontier systems are more accurate and run at
high reasoning (median $`\sim`$2,000 reasoning tokens/request; Table
[H.2](#A8.T2 "Table H.2 ‣ H.2 Frontier Model Reasoning Usage ‣ Appendix H Prompting and Extended Experiments ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
but their accept/reject recalls are skewed. Gemini-3.1-Pro accepts only
30–34% of papers in three of four settings, while GPT-5.5 swings between
accepting 39% and 74%.

The coding-agent rows test whether interactive access to both modalities
changes this pattern. While Claude Code has the strongest rating
correlation and the agents have among the strongest AUCs in the baseline
block, their Acc is lower than the best non-agent frontier baselines.
Like Jev, coding agents can rank papers in a way that agrees with
reviewer ratings, but still turn that ranking into skewed accept/reject
decisions. DeepReview generates review-style judgments and a meta-review
decision; its 14B model improves over 7B but still trails the best
frontier model and PaperScorer.

Binary SFT recovers a stronger decision signal. The central result in
Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
is that direct accept/reject supervision gives the strongest decision
predictor and ranking signal. On ICLR, PaperScorer-Vision reaches
$`68.3`$ Acc, $`2.7\%`$ ahead of the best frontier vision model,
Gemini-3-Flash. On arXiv, the matched arXiv-trained PaperScorer-Vision
reaches $`77.5`$, a larger $`9.0\%`$ ahead of the best frontier
baseline. On both datasets, PaperScorer-Vision significantly beats both
large frontier models in Acc and AUC (one-sided paired bootstrap,
$`p<.05`$; [Appendix
J](#A10 "Appendix J Statistical Uncertainty ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
These gains are not a threshold artifact, since PaperScorer-Vision keeps
accept and reject recall balanced, while the frontier systems rank
papers well but natively skew their decisions.

Figure 5: Binary SFT is strongest over time. PaperScorer-Text and
PaperScorer-Vision use matched-source training. Across years, supervised
PaperScorer leads Acc/AUC, vision is strongest, and RL trails prompting
frontier models.

Figure
[5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
shows that the modality and method ordering is stable across years, with
PaperScorer-Vision best in every matched-source year, prompting
intermediate, and RL weaker. These results indicate that papers carry
recoverable decision signal, although learning that signal through long
reasoning traces is difficult with only a single, noisy accept/reject
bit as reward. Supervising directly on the final decision works better,
and vision keeps the layout and presentation cues that a markdown
extract would strip.

Accuracy is not constant over time, and Acc and AUC drop sharply from
’25 to ’26 across PaperScorer, frontier models, and DeepReview,
suggesting a shared change in the evaluation distribution. The
early-cycle arXiv ’26 slice is also small, with 198 test papers from
AAAI, CVPR, and ICLR ’26. Each cycle also introduces new methods,
benchmarks, and reviewer norms that reset what counts as a strong paper,
so some recalibration is unavoidable for any predictor whose training
pool is more than a year stale. Training only through ’25 transfers
poorly to ’26 ([Appendix
F.2](#A6.SS2 "F.2 Ablating Training Distribution and Paper Representation ‣ Appendix F Training Variations ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
so we fold ’26 into training and expect any deployed predictor to be
periodically retrained as new conferences land.

Beyond hard decisions, both PaperScorer-Text and PaperScorer-Vision
reach top AUC on both datasets, ranking accepts above rejects regardless
of threshold. The score also tracks human ratings; on ICLR,
PaperScorer-Vision’s $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ correlates with reviewer
ratings more closely than DeepReview and frontier baselines, despite
training only on final decisions. arXiv ratings are sparser
($`292`$/$`\sim`$$`1{,}415`$ test papers, skewed toward NeurIPS and ICLR
accepts); on that biased subset coding agents correlate with ratings
better than PaperScorer but still make worse decisions, so correlation
with reviewer ratings does not convert into correct accept/reject calls.

Model and data scale. Model scale changes decision accuracy only
modestly once the SFT objective is fixed (Figure
[6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")a).
Relative to matched 7B checkpoints, 3B and 14B variants barely move Acc,
with no consistent direction across modality or source. A paired 95%
bootstrap CI reveals that nearly every change in Acc is statistically
insignificant (shaded in Figure
[6(a)](#S4.F6.sf1 "Figure 6(a) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
Vision is similarly competitive at smaller scale, so in Figure
[6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")b
the largest arXiv Acc gain comes from data scale rather than parameter
scale.

For ICLR, we vary dataset size from 50% to 75% of the full pool. For
arXiv, the arXiv-m and arXiv sets give us a 3.4$`\times`$ multiple. More
data helps for both datasets, and Figure
[6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")b
shows that the dominant arXiv gain is data scale, not parameter scale,
as the curve climbs steeply from arXiv-m to arXiv, well past the spread
of the 3B/7B/14B parameter sweep. ICLR is much smaller, so taking 50%
and 75% of this population compresses the visible slope, and the curves
should not be read as comparable in absolute terms.

Figure 7: Vision is strongest on average. Points show the benefit of

Vision is strongest. It improves over text in the average ICLR/arXiv
view (Figure
[7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"))
and in almost every dataset-specific comparison
([Table J.2](#A10.T2 "In Appendix J Statistical Uncertainty ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
For PaperScorer, the Vision row beats its Text row on both datasets, and
a paired bootstrap confirms the gain ($`p=.012`$ and $`.005`$ after
Holm–Bonferroni correction ([Abdi, 2010](#bib.bib1))). For the frontier
families, the vision–text gaps are small and none is significant once
their decisions are thresholded ([Appendix
J](#A10 "Appendix J Statistical Uncertainty ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
Screenshots preserve complete figures and tables, equation layout, and
visual polish, all of which markdown extraction discards.

Second, the signal largely survives heavy compression, since tiling all
ten PaperScorer-Vision pages into a single 2380$`\times`$1512 image cuts
vision tokens by about $`63\%`$ (roughly $`12{,}420`$ to $`4{,}590`$),
and only drops performance on ICLR by 2.2% (Table
[4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
a small change relative to the $`>60\%`$ token cut.

To investigate vision’s consistent advantage and the small cost of
compression, we asked the base VL backbone to perform OCR on each input.
On per-page screenshots it recovers $`{\sim}80\%`$ of the content
verbatim against the markdown extract. On the compressed panel, OCR
retention drops to $`{\sim}30\%`$. Compression sharply reduces
recoverable text while preserving layout, figure placement, and overall
visual presentation. Prior work supports this direction, as diagram
count and quality correlate with citations ([Marshall et al.,
2021](#bib.bib30)), and paper organization shapes peer-review outcomes
([Jung et al., 2025](#bib.bib22)).

## Section 5 Where does this signal lie?

Having shown that paper content carries a recoverable, well-ranked
decision signal, we now ask *where* that signal lives, across confidence
ranges, papers, and conferences.

Figure 8: Calibration on both datasets. Reliability (confidence vs.
accuracy, $`y{=}x`$ dotted) on the balanced ICLR (left) and arXiv
(right) test sets for PaperScorer text and vision and for Jev, after
temperature scaling. Dashed lines show the cumulative coverage (share of
test papers at or above each confidence).

Confidence tracks accuracy. Like most modern neural networks ([Guo et
al., 2017](#bib.bib15)), ours are mildly overconfident, with raw accept
probabilities higher than their accuracy warrants, so we correct them
with temperature scaling ([Guo et al., 2017](#bib.bib15)). For each
paper $`i`$ we take the model’s *accept log-odds*
$`\ell_{i}=\log P(\text{Accept})-\log P(\text{Reject})`$ from the
decision-token log-probabilities, and fit a temperature $`\tau`$ for the
calibrated accept probability $`p_{\mathrm{cal}}`$ by minimizing its
negative log-likelihood, where $`z_{i}\in\{0,1\}`$ is the decision:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{\mathrm{cal}}=\sigma\big(\ell_{i}/\tau+\log(\pi/(1-\pi))\big),\qquad\mathcal{L}(\tau)=-\sum_{i}\big[z_{i}\log p_{\mathrm{cal}}+(1-z_{i})\log(1-p_{\mathrm{cal}})\big].
``` |  |

Here, $`\pi`$ is the acceptance rate of the scored papers. We fit
$`\tau`$ on a natural-rate validation split with $`\pi`$ set to its
acceptance rate, so the shift handles the base rate and $`\tau`$ only
sets sharpness. On our balanced test sets $`\pi=0.5`$ and the shift
vanishes. Neither changes a decision (Accept iff $`\ell_{i}\geq 0`$,
i.e. $`p_{\mathrm{cal}}\geq\pi`$), so Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
is unchanged. Confidence is $`c=p_{\mathrm{cal}}`$ for an Accept and
$`1-p_{\mathrm{cal}}`$ for a Reject. Jev’s scores already sit near the
real acceptance rate, so we fit its $`\tau`$ without the shift and apply
the correction in reverse on our 50/50 test sets.

After scaling, both PaperScorer models track the $`y{=}x`$ line on both
datasets (Figure
[8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Section 5 Where does this signal lie? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
so their confidence matches their accuracy, and Jev, corrected the same
way, is roughly calibrated too (ECE $`.05`$ and $`.02`$, vs.
$`.02`$–$`.03`$ for ours). The difference is how often each model is
confident (dashed coverage curves). At 70% confidence or more,
PaperScorer covers about a third of ICLR papers and over half of arXiv
papers, at nearly 80% and 85% accuracy, while Jev covers only 6% and
12%.

Deployment at the real acceptance rate. Most papers are rejected, and a
venue’s rate $`\pi`$ can be estimated from previous years. Adding
$`\log(\pi/(1-\pi))`$ to $`\ell`$ gives acceptance probabilities at that
rate, cutting calibration error from .13 to .02–.03. At ICLR’s rate,
Accept calls are right 47% of the time and Reject calls 82% ([Appendix
I.3](#A9.SS3 "I.3 Calibration Details ‣ Appendix I SFT and RL Method Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

(a) Accuracy by rating percentile (ICLR).

![Refer to caption](2610.31791v1/selective_reliability_rating_b.png)

(b) Rating $`\times`$ confidence $`\to`$ accuracy (ICLR).

its own conference and year. (a) Frontier models recognize low-rated
papers but fail on the high-rated ones, whereas PaperScorer-Vision is
accurate at both tails, while all models are weak in the middle. (b) The
same shape as a confidence/rating surface, with a deep dip in the
$`[0.4,0.5]`$ rating slice and the high-accuracy, high-confidence region
concentrated on the tail papers.

Selective reliability. ICLR has human ground-truth ratings for each
paper, so we can measure accuracy at each level of the human rating
(Figure
[9](#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Section 5 Where does this signal lie? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")a).
Every model is most accurate at the lowest-rated papers and near chance
in the middle of the rating range. The models differ at the top end,
where PaperScorer-Vision stays accurate on the highest-rated papers
while GPT and Gemini fall off, so the frontier models accurately predict
the lowest-rated papers but fail on the highest-rated ones. Conditioning
jointly on rating and confidence (Figure
[9](#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Section 5 Where does this signal lie? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")b)
shows the same shape, with accuracy peaking on the confident extremes
and collapsing in the middle, where none of the evaluated models finds
enough signal.

Performance across conferences. Accuracy varies sharply by venue (Figure
[10](#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Section 5 Where does this signal lie? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
On six of the seven highest-coverage venues, PaperScorer-Vision matches
or beats the best frontier model (Gemini-3.1-Pro or GPT-5.5). The
exceptions are the vision-heavy CV venues, where the frontier models
perform particularly well. Gemini ties PaperScorer on CVPR and is the
most accurate model on ICCV, the only high-coverage venue where a
frontier model wins. AAAI is the other extreme, with PaperScorer near
$`90`$ while both frontier models fall close to chance, the widest gap.
AAAI accepts and rejects run equally long, so the gap is not a length
effect; PaperScorer ranks them more cleanly here than anywhere else.
In-domain training therefore gives PaperScorer a clear edge everywhere
except the visual CV papers, where strong general vision models compete.

Figure 10: Accuracy by venue. The best frontier vision models
(Gemini-3.1-Pro, GPT-5.5) against PaperScorer-Vision on arXiv by venue.
PaperScorer leads on all high-coverage venues but CVPR and ICCV, where
Gemini ties or leads.

## Section 6 Related Work

Paper acceptance prediction and dataset construction. Paper outcome
prediction predates modern language models, with early work using
bibliometric, lexical, and handcrafted signals ([Yan et al.,
2011](#bib.bib47); [Zhao et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [Hull and Bihlo,
2025](#bib.bib19)). Recent datasets and methods move closer to
paper-level accept/reject prediction, including PeerRead ([Kang et al.,
2018](#bib.bib23)), Deep Paper Gestalt ([Huang, 2018](#bib.bib18)),
DeepReview ([Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib56)), ScholarPeer ([Goyal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14)), and Sakana’s AI Reviewer ([Lu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)). The main challenge is label provenance, since prior
sources mix arXiv, LaTeX, and OpenReview artifacts ([Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib56)), compare camera-ready accepts against anonymized
rejects ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib28)), or use workshop papers as
reject proxies ([Huang, 2018](#bib.bib18)). These choices can make
labels recoverable from source, venue, or revision artifacts (audited in
[Appendix
B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Shortcuts in Prior Datasets ‣ Appendix B Data Curation Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"));
we instead construct datasets in which the label is recoverable only
from the paper’s content.

Review generation and reviewer agents. A parallel line of work studies
critique generation, review quality, reviewer agreement, and multi-agent
review simulation rather than direct final-decision prediction.
Reviewer2 ([Gao et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)) analyzes reviewer behavior
and agreement. DeepReview ([Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib56)), ReviewRL
([Zeng et al., 2025](#bib.bib51)), and OpenReviewer ([Idahl and Ahmadi,
2025](#bib.bib20)) generate review-style outputs, while AgentReview
([Jin et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)), the Stanford Agentic Reviewer
([PaperReview.ai, 2025](#bib.bib34)), MARG ([D’Arcy et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10)), MAMORX ([Taechoyotin et al., 2024](#bib.bib39)), and
ScholarPeer ([Goyal et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)) move toward agentic
reviewing. These systems need reliable decision priors because generated
critiques can be persuasive, yet when conditioned on the wrong prior
they can lead to drastically different comments and decisions. We
therefore ask whether a calibrated acceptance probability improves
agentic reviewing ([Appendix
K](#A11 "Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

AI-assisted scientific workflows. Automated reviewing is also becoming
part of larger scientific workflows. Systems such as The AI Scientist
v1/v2 ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Yamada et al.,
2025](#bib.bib46)), CycleResearcher ([Weng et al., 2025](#bib.bib44)),
FunSearch ([Romera-Paredes et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)), AlphaEvolve
([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)), and execution-grounded research
agents ([Si et al., 2026](#bib.bib37)) use model-based evaluation to
filter ideas, judge generated artifacts, or steer search. AstaBench
([Bragg et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)) formalizes evaluation for the full
idea-to-paper setting. In these pipelines, reviewer models act as
selection mechanisms rather than summarizers, so systematic accept bias
or poor calibration can shape which research directions are pursued.
This motivates PaperScorer as a calibrated decision prior for both
retrieval and review assistance ([Appendix
K](#A11 "Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

## Section 7 Conclusion and Applications

We introduce PaperScorer, a family of text and vision models that
predict a paper’s final accept/reject decision from its content alone.
Tested on ICLR and source-derived arXiv papers, supervised binary
prediction recovers a strong paper-level signal, and 7B vision
PaperScorer models outperform frontier reasoning and DeepReview
baselines on decision accuracy and ranking, while producing calibrated
acceptance probabilities. We find that paper artifacts contain
substantial recoverable decision signal. Screenshots of the paper
preserve layout, figure, and presentation cues that markdown extraction
tends to discard.

PaperScorer is not a replacement for peer review or a universal measure
of scientific value. Its best use is as a calibrated estimate of
acceptance probability that larger scientific workflows can use as a
prior, which we demonstrate in two settings ([Appendix
K](#A11 "Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
In literature retrieval, combining dense semantic retrieval scores from
an embedding model with PaperScorer-Vision’s acceptance score surfaces
papers that are both semantically relevant and likely to be accepted. On
the LitSearch benchmark, this improves ground-truth citation recall in
the top-10 results by 8.7%. In agentic reviewing, conditioning Claude
Code on the PaperScorer-Vision prior raises decision accuracy from 63.0%
to 70.6% and improves alignment with human reviews, mainly by correcting
the agent’s incorrect acceptance predictions.

## Section 8 Limitations and Future Work

We cannot yet say *why* the model favors one paper over another. Our
attention maps and section-edit tests ([Appendix
L.1](#A12.SS1 "L.1 Section-Attention Map ‣ Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"))
show what it reads, but they do not *establish causality*, and they rely
on last-layer attention from only a few papers. The idea that vision
performs better by capturing a paper’s overall look remains a
conjecture, supported but not settled by our compression and modality
results. The model also weakens on the newest papers, where our data is
thin. By ’26, some decisions reflect AI help as much as human judgment,
and dropping ’26 from training lowers accuracy ([Appendix
F.2](#A6.SS2 "F.2 Ablating Training Distribution and Paper Representation ‣ Appendix F Training Variations ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
That year is also unusual, with shorter rebuttals, the narrowest
accept-reject rating gap we have seen, and arXiv labels from only a few
venues. This should ease as more ’26 papers appear, and PaperScorer can
be retrained through our pipeline.

What the score captures. A high $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ predicts the
accept/reject outcome; it is not a measure of novelty or long-term
impact, and it comes with no explanation of *why* (though it does have
correlations to reviewer rating and citation count). On impact, the one
slice with both full reviewer ratings and citations, ICLR ’25, is
encouraging, as $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ tracks later citations about as
well as the human review score does ($`\rho\approx.25`$ for both,
[Appendix
J](#A10 "Appendix J Statistical Uncertainty ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
though one conference-year and small sample make this a preliminary
result. The model itself provides no explanation for its prediction, so
any reasoning for a decision must be generated afterward, by the model
or an agentic reviewer. Conditioning a reviewer on
$`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ raises agreement with human reviews ([Appendix
K.2](#A11.SS2 "K.2 Grounding Agentic Reviewers ‣ Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
but such post-hoc rationales can hallucinate. A more robust path likely
needs multi-agent generation with verification loops.

Future work. The clearest next steps are expanding high-fidelity
datasets across more venues, improving borderline-paper modeling, and
developing richer supervision than a single binary outcome, especially
for cases where reviewer disagreement and venue-specific norms matter.

  §

## Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation

We follow the NeurIPS ’14 / ’21 consistency experiment ([Beygelzimer et
al., 2021](#bib.bib5)), where each paper $`i`$ is reviewed by two
committees $`j\in\{1,2\}`$ with independent decisions conditional on a
latent acceptance probability $`p_{i}\sim F`$ (step
[a](#A1.Ex7 "Equation a ‣ Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
Here $`F`$ is the (unknown) population distribution of per-paper
acceptance probabilities, whose first two moments we estimate from the
consistency experiment below. The experiment’s reported acceptance rate
of $`{\approx}\,26\%`$ fixes the first moment (step
[b](#A1.Ex8 "Equation b ‣ Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
and its disagreement rate of $`{\approx}\,23\%`$ corresponds to
$`\mathbb{E}[2p(1-p)]`$ (step
[c](#A1.Ex9 "Equation c ‣ Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
which expands into the second moment and variance (steps
[d](#A1.Ex10 "Equation d ‣ Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"),
[e](#A1.Ex11 "Equation e ‣ Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
Matching these to a Beta family (steps
[f](#A1.Ex12 "Equation f ‣ Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"),
[g](#A1.Ex13 "Equation g ‣ Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"))
gives $`(\alpha,\beta)\approx(0.39,1.10)`$. Under the natural acceptance
distribution, the Bayes-optimal predictor accepts when $`p>0.5`$, giving
$`\mathrm{Acc}^{\star}\approx 83.3\%`$ (step
[h](#A1.Ex14 "Equation h ‣ Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle D_{j}^{(i)}`$ | $`\displaystyle\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_{i}),\qquad j\in\{1,2\}`$ |  | (a) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[p]`$ | $`\displaystyle=0.26`$ |  | (b) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[2p(1-p)]`$ | $`\displaystyle=0.23`$ |  | (c) |
|  | $`\displaystyle 2\mathbb{E}[p]-2\mathbb{E}[p^{2}]`$ | $`\displaystyle=0.23\;\Longrightarrow\;\mathbb{E}[p^{2}]=\frac{0.52-0.23}{2}=0.145`$ |  | (d) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(p)`$ | $`\displaystyle=0.145-0.26^{2}\approx 0.077`$ |  | (e) |
|  | $`\displaystyle p`$ | $`\displaystyle\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),\qquad\tfrac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}=0.26,\;\;\tfrac{\alpha(\alpha+1)}{(\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+\beta+1)}=0.145`$ |  | (f) |
|  | $`\displaystyle(\alpha,\beta)`$ | $`\displaystyle\approx(0.39,1.10)`$ |  | (g) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Acc}^{\star}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\max(p,1-p)]\approx 83.3\%`$ |  | (h) |
|  | $`\displaystyle p\mid D{=}1`$ | $`\displaystyle\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1.39,1.10),\quad p\mid D{=}0\sim\mathrm{Beta}(0.39,2.10)`$ |  | (i) |
|  | $`\displaystyle P(\mathrm{accept}\mid p)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\tfrac{\beta p}{\beta p+\alpha(1-p)}=0.5\;\;\text{at}\;\;p=\tfrac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}=0.26`$ |  | (j) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Acc}^{\star}_{\mathrm{balanced}}`$ | $`\displaystyle\approx 80.2\%`$ |  | (k) |

Our evaluation uses a balanced 50/50 pool of accepted and rejected
papers, so the relevant ceiling differs. Beta-Bernoulli conjugacy gives
the conditional posteriors in step
[i](#A1.Ex15 "Equation i ‣ Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"),
and under a uniform 50/50 class prior the posterior accept probability
(step
[j](#A1.Ex16 "Equation j ‣ Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"))
equals $`0.5`$ exactly at $`p=\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)=0.26`$. The
Bayes-optimal rule in the balanced setting therefore predicts accept
when $`p>0.26`$. Averaging over the two conditional Beta distributions
yields the balanced ceiling in step
[k](#A1.Ex17 "Equation k ‣ Appendix A Bayesian Optimal Accuracy Derivation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"),
the value reported in the main text.

## Appendix B Data Curation Details

### B.1 Shortcuts in Prior Datasets

Existing accept/reject datasets often mix artifacts in ways that make
labels recoverable from source, venue, or revision artifacts rather than
from the paper’s content. For instance, Deep Paper Gestalt ([Huang,
2018](#bib.bib18)) pairs accepted CVPR papers against workshop papers as
a reject pool, but the workshop format alone (shorter page count,
distinct headers) is enough to shortcut the prediction problem without
ever reading the paper. We compare three public datasets, DeepReview
’24–’25 ([Zhu et al., 2025](#bib.bib56)), Sakana’s AI Scientist ’22 ([Lu
et al., 2024](#bib.bib28)), and our raw ICLR ’24 (before normalization),
against the selected PaperScorer years. We tested several signals
defined in
[Table B.1](#A2.T1 "In B.1 Shortcuts in Prior Datasets ‣ Appendix B Data Curation Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"),
and
[Table B.2](#A2.T2 "In B.1 Shortcuts in Prior Datasets ‣ Appendix B Data Curation Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
reports accept/reject percentages (A/R) for each.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Signal |  Definition |
|  Markdown / LaTeX source |  Native source artifacts (e.g. \begin{equation}, \cite) survive in the text, indicating the dataset retained LaTeX source rather than rendering to PDF. |
|  Author names visible |  Non-anonymous author block present before the abstract. |
|  Affil. before abstract |  Institutional affiliation visible in the front matter before the abstract. |
|  Has ack. |  An Acknowledgments section heading is present anywhere in the paper. |
|  Affil. in ack. |  Institutional affiliation strings appear inside the Acknowledgments section. |
|  GitHub in abstract |  A GitHub URL appears in the abstract text. |

Table B.1: Identity-leaking signals tested in the artifact shortcut
audit. Each signal is a heuristic that, if positively correlated with
the accept/reject label, lets a classifier shortcut the prediction
problem from formatting alone.

Among the comparators, DeepReview ’24 carries source for 78.7% of
accepts but only 41.2% of rejects, a strong leakage shortcut. AI
Scientist ’22 has 100% of accept papers with visible author names
against essentially zero reject papers, because the rejects come from
anonymized OpenReview submissions while the accepts are camera-ready
PDFs. Our selected years stay at most 0.92% A / 1.73% R on any signal.
Our audit shows that sourcing papers from the latest pre-camera-ready
rebuttal artifact does not suffer from any of these shortcuts.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Signal |  DeepReview ’24 |  DeepReview ’25 |  AI Scientist ’22 |  Ours raw ’24 |  Ours selected years |
| Markdown / LaTeX source | 78.7 / 41.2 | 53.0 / 37.8 | 0.0 / 0.0 | 0.0 / 0.0 | 0.01 / 0.0 |
| Author names visible | 0.0 / 0.0 | 0.0 / 0.0 | 100.0 / 0.6 | 99.7 / 0.4 | 0.0 / 0.0 |
| Affil. before abs. | 0.7 / 0.2 | 0.4 / 0.2 | 53.8 / 0.0 | 51.1 / 0.04 | 0.0 / 0.0 |
| Has ack. | 16.4 / 2.8 | 4.9 / 2.8 | 74.5 / 2.8 | 73.9 / 1.7 | 0.92 / 1.73 |
| Affil. in ack. | 4.4 / 1.1 | 1.3 / 0.6 | 48.9 / 0.9 | 31.8 / 0.1 | 0.07 / 0.20 |
| GitHub in abs. | 4.0 / 0.5 | 0.5 / 0.5 | 0.0 / 0.0 | 22.5 / 1.1 | 0.0 / 0.0 |

Table B.2: Artifact shortcut audit across public paper datasets. We
measure accept/reject percentages (A/R) of source, author, affiliation,
acknowledgment, and code-leakage signals. The selected PaperScorer years
avoid these shortcuts, while raw ICLR ’24 shows why camera-ready accepts
remain problematic.

Why we exclude ICLR ’24. For ’24, neither the initial submission nor the
latest rebuttal PDF is publicly available, so the only artifact we can
recover is the camera-ready version of accepts paired with the latest
rebuttal of rejects. We attempted to recover an anonymized version of
ICLR ’24 by performing manual anonymization on the camera-ready PDF. We
strip identity-bearing spans from text and whiten the same regions in
rendered pages, but the camera-ready transition still shifts page layout
and section start positions
([Figure B.1](#A2.F1 "In B.2 Data Provenance and Ensuring Anonymity ‣ Appendix B Data Curation Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
Vision picks this up. Even after normalization, the model remains
unusually strong on ’24, indicating that residual layout cues survive
whiteout. MinerU confirms the source of the problem. Across years, the
mean $`y`$-position of the introduction start is roughly matched between
accepts and rejects, except in ’24 where the gap is notable. This is
consistent with author-block expansion, GitHub insertion, and whitespace
changes after masking, which is why ’24 is excluded from the benchmark
and training pool.

Figure B.1: Why normalized ICLR ’24 remains shortcut-prone for vision.
We strip identity-bearing spans from text and whiten the same regions in
rendered pages, but the camera-ready transition still shifts page layout
and section start positions. Text mostly tolerates this cleanup; vision
does not.

### B.3 Our Data Pipeline

We run two independent workflows that produce two independent datasets.
The ICLR workflow downloads ICLR submissions and decisions directly from
OpenReview, runs MinerU, redacts identity, and subsamples. The arXiv
workflow recovers both the venue and the decision from each paper’s
arXiv source tarball and matches against public paperlists.
[Figures 2(a)](#A2.F2.sf1 "In Figure B.2 ‣ B.2 Data Provenance and Ensuring Anonymity ‣ Appendix B Data Curation Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
and [2(b)](#A2.F2.sf2 "Figure 2(b) ‣ Figure B.2 ‣ B.2 Data Provenance and Ensuring Anonymity ‣ Appendix B Data Curation Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
show the two funnels, and
[Table B.5](#A2.T5 "In B.3 Our Data Pipeline ‣ Appendix B Data Curation Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
summarizes the final canonical training pools used throughout the paper.

|         |        |        |        |                        |
|---------|--------|--------|--------|------------------------|
| Source  | Total  | Accept | Reject | Train / Val / Test     |
| ICLR    | 24,888 | 12,442 | 12,446 | 21,141 / 1,252 / 2,495 |
| arXiv   | 83,656 | 41,828 | 41,828 | 71,124 / 4,174 / 8,358 |
| arXiv-m | 24,650 | 12,325 | 12,325 | 20,962 / 1,232 / 2,456 |

Table B.5: Canonical training datasets. ICLR is per-year 50:50 balanced
across ’20–’23 and ’25–’26 (’24 excluded). arXiv is per-venue 50:50
balanced across NeurIPS, CVPR, NLP, AAAI, ICLR, ICML, and other ML
venues. arXiv-m is a proportional per-venue subsample of arXiv used
throughout the paper for compute-matched ablations.

##### ICLR.

We pull every ICLR submission in OpenReview for ’20–’26 (45,328 papers)
and, per year, the latest publicly available pre-camera-ready PDF. PDFs
run through MinerU to obtain markdown and per-page images, then we
redact identity-bearing spans (author block, affiliations,
acknowledgments, GitHub links). After joining with reviews and decisions
and applying an 85/5/10 stratified split balanced per (year, decision)
cell, we obtain 24,888 papers (’20: 1,367; ’21: 1,610; ’22: 2,154; ’23:
3,088; ’25: 6,790; ’26: 9,879).

##### arXiv.

We start from 434,579 ML arXiv papers spanning ’20–’26 by update date.
We pull source directly from arXiv’s requester-pays S3 mirror
(s3://arxiv/src/) for every paper from January ’20 through our 05/01/’26
cutoff, and use NeMo Curator’s vendored ArxivIterator ([NVIDIA,
2024](#bib.bib33)) to walk each monthly tar and recover the per-paper
.tex contents. We then scan every .tex against our tracked-venue
templates and keep only the tarballs that match a known venue style
file. The workflow detects the submission venue from the LaTeX source
via these venue-specific style files, strips identity-bearing spans
directly from the LaTeX source (author block, affiliations,
acknowledgments, GitHub links) and recompiles the PDF, runs MinerU, and
matches each in-pool paper against every venue paperlist in the public
Paper Copilot index ([Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib50)) within a $`Y{-}5`$
to $`Y{+}2`$ year window. Papers that template for a venue with
ground-truth but find no paperlist match are tagged as implied rejects
and kept, unless they trigger a workshop, short-paper, or
no-ground-truth filter that drops them. Per-venue 50:50 balancing with a
stratified 85/5/10 split yields the arXiv dataset of 83,656 papers
spanning NeurIPS, CVPR, ACL, AAAI, ICLR, ICML, and other ML venues.
Throughout the paper we use the full arXiv set. For compute-matched
ablations, we use the subsample arXiv-m, produced by proportional
per-(venue, label) downsampling of arXiv to 24,650 papers.

## Appendix C Simple Feature Analysis

|  Feature |  Definition | $`\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{ICLR}}`$ | $`\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{arXiv}}`$ |

|  Ablation mentions |  Set to 1 if lowercase text contains ablation, otherwise 0. | +0.09 | +0.14 |
|  Abstract sent. length |  Average sentence length (in words) of the abstract. | +0.12 | $`-`$0.01 |
|  Abstract sentence count |  Number of sentences in the abstract. | +0.23 | $`-`$0.01 |
|  Abstract words |  Number of whitespace-delimited words in the abstract. | $`-`$0.14 | +0.04 |
|  Algorithms per pg. |  Count case-sensitive matches of the pattern Algorithm followed by whitespace and a digit, then divide by the estimated body-page proxy. | $`-`$0.03 | +0.03 |
|  Appendix refs. per pg. |  Count case-sensitive matches of Appendix followed by whitespace and a capital letter, then divide by the estimated body-page proxy. | +0.13 | +0.10 |
|  Baseline mention |  Set to 1 if lowercase text contains baseline, otherwise 0. |  0.00 | +0.07 |
|  Benchmark mention |  Set to 1 if lowercase text contains benchmark, otherwise 0. | $`-`$0.01 | +0.03 |
|  Citation-year count |  Detect four-digit year strings in the extracted text, keep years in \[1990, 2026\], and compute log(1 + number of retained year strings). | +0.10 | $`-`$0.01 |

|  Proposal mentions |  Count lowercase regex matches of words beginning with propos. | $`-`$0.05 | $`-`$0.01 |
|  Rare-word ratio |  From the first 5,000 lowercased alphabetic words, compute the number of unique words that appear exactly once divided by max(number of unique words, 1). | $`-`$0.14 | $`-`$0.06 |
|  Recent citation share |  Detect four-digit year strings in the extracted text, keep years in \[1990, 2026\], and compute count(years \>= 2024) divided by max(number of retained year strings, 1). | +0.09 | $`-`$0.15 |
|  Related work |  Set to 1 if lowercase text contains related work, otherwise 0. | +0.02 | +0.09 |
|  Reproducibility indicator |  Set to 1 if lowercase text matches reproduc, code followed later by avail, or open followed by one character then sourc, otherwise 0. | $`-`$0.02 | $`-`$0.06 |
|  RL terms/1k words |  Count case-insensitive matches of these reinforcement-learning terms: reinforcement learning, reward, policy gradient, MDP, Q-learning, actor critic, environment, agent, exploration, exploitation, Atari, MuJoCo. Divide by max(total word count, 1) and multiply by 1,000. | $`-`$0.02 | $`-`$0.07 |
|  Sections per pg. |  Count Markdown headings that start a line with one to three hash marks followed by whitespace, then divide by the estimated body-page proxy. | $`-`$0.08 | $`-`$0.15 |
|  Self-references/1k words |  Count these lowercase phrases: our method, our approach, our model, our framework, our algorithm, our technique, our work, our paper, and our contribution. Divide by max(total word count, 1) and multiply by 1,000. | +0.01 | +0.08 |
|  Self-supervised topic terms |  Count case-insensitive matches of these self-supervised/contrastive-learning terms: self supervised, contrastive, SimCLR, BYOL, MoCo, pretext task, representation learning, unsupervised pre. Divide by max(total word count, 1) and multiply by 1,000. | +0.03 | +0.02 |
|  Sentence length |  Split the extracted text on periods, exclamation marks, and question marks, keep spans longer than 10 characters, and compute total whitespace-delimited word count divided by max(number of retained spans, 1). | $`-`$0.18 | $`-`$0.24 |
|  Sentence-length variation |  Split the extracted text into retained sentences as above, compute the standard deviation of sentence word counts, and divide by max(avg_sentence_length, 1). | +0.02 | +0.04 |
|  Significance mentions |  Set to 1 if lowercase text matches statistic followed later by signific, p followed by one character then value, confidence interval, standard deviation, or error bar, otherwise 0. | $`-`$0.01 | $`-`$0.03 |
|  Speech topic terms |  Count case-insensitive matches of these speech/audio terms: speech, audio, acoustic, spectrogram, ASR, TTS, voice, phoneme, waveform. Divide by max(total word count, 1) and multiply by 1,000. | +0.01 |  0.00 |
|  Table refs. per pg. |  Count case-sensitive matches of Table followed by whitespace and a digit, then divide by the estimated body-page proxy. | $`-`$0.03 | +0.06 |
|  Theory markers |  Count case-sensitive matches of Theorem, Lemma, Proposition, Corollary, Definition, and Proof. | +0.03 | +0.06 |
|  Theory topic terms |  Count case-insensitive matches of these theory/proof/bound terms: theorem, proof, lemma, proposition, corollary, bound, complexity, PAC, VC dimension, Rademacher, concentration inequality. Divide by max(total word count, 1) and multiply by 1,000. | +0.07 | +0.01 |
|  Title colon |  Set to 1 if the extracted title contains a colon, otherwise 0. | +0.05 | +0.05 |
|  Title length |  Use metadata title when available, otherwise the first Markdown H1 heading, and count characters. | $`-`$0.07 | +0.01 |

Table C.1: Programmatic feature inventory. We compute each probe feature
from the concatenated human-side paper text, truncated to the first
80,000 characters. In feature names, per pg. means per estimated body
page.

The main text reports the top five accept- and reject-associated
features from separate ICLR and arXiv feature probes in
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.2 A Simple Paper Features Baseline ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?").
[Table C.1](#A3.T1 "In Appendix C Simple Feature Analysis ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
lists every feature in the probe with its definition. The columns
$`w_{\mathrm{ICLR}}`$ and $`w_{\mathrm{arXiv}}`$ are the signed
standardized coefficients from logistic-regression probes trained on all
features against the ICLR and arXiv decision label, respectively. The
probe excludes source identifiers, direct venue labels, ratings,
citations, author names, and non-comparable body-page counts. The
strongest individual signal — paper length on both sources — saturates
at $`w\approx+0.48`$, an order of magnitude below what PaperScorer
achieves end-to-end. Reject-side magnitudes are smaller still
($`|w|\leq 0.25`$), and most features sit between $`-0.05`$ and
$`+0.10`$, indicating that simple structural shortcuts do not cleanly
separate accept from reject.

## Appendix D Do Frontier Models Memorize the Test Decisions?

GPT-5.5’s December ’25 knowledge cutoff postdates the public release of
ICLR ’25 decisions and most of our arXiv test years, so a natural worry
is that its baseline accuracy comes from remembering outcomes rather
than judging papers. Gemini-3.1-Pro (January ’25 cutoff) predates both.
We test this in two steps. First, we ask whether the models remember our
test papers at all. Second, and more importantly, we ask whether
remembering a paper makes the model any more accurate on it.

##### Do the models remember the papers?

We sample 200 papers per corpus (100 accepted, 100 rejected) from the
papers on which GPT-5.5 is evaluated in
[Table 3](#S4.T3 "In 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"),
so that every probed paper also has a prediction from the main table.
Each paper is probed with five *label-recall* cues that ask the model
whether it remembers the paper’s decision:

- •
  title — title only.
- •
  title_abstract — title plus abstract.
- •
  mc — multiple choice among accept, reject, and a distractor, given the
  title and abstract.
- •
  continuation — the first sentence after the abstract, asking whether
  the model recognizes the paper.
- •
  web_search_framing — a prompt phrased as if the model could look up
  the venue and outcome.

For each cue we report the *claim rate*, the fraction of papers where
the model says it remembers the decision, and the *outcome accuracy when
claimed*. A sixth *content-recall* cue asks the model to continue the
abstract from its title, scored by ROUGE-L ([Lin, 2004](#bib.bib27)).
Gemini-3.1-Pro was probed on an earlier 50-paper draw per corpus with
the same cues.

[Table D.1](#A4.T1 "In Does remembering a paper help? ‣ Appendix D Do Frontier Models Memorize the Test Decisions? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
shows that GPT-5.5 does recognize many of our test papers, and that
recognition follows its cutoff exactly. On ICLR, the title cue is
claimed for 30% of ’25 papers but only 7% of ’26 papers, and on arXiv
for 44% of ’24 papers but 17% of ’25 and 23% of ’26. Gemini-3.1-Pro
claims recall for at most 4% of ICLR papers under any cue. Recognition
is not the same as remembering the decision, however. When GPT-5.5
claims to recall a decision it is right only 50–73% of the time, and
this is inflated by an accept bias: it says “accept” for 65% of the ICLR
papers it claims to remember, so balanced accuracy over its claimed
decisions is 44%, no better than chance. Content recall is absent: mean
ROUGE-L on abstract continuation is $`\leq 0.004`$ on every slice and no
paper reaches $`0.5`$.

##### Does remembering a paper help?

If GPT-5.5 were retrieving remembered decisions, it would be more
accurate on the papers it recognizes. We split each probed corpus into
papers it claimed to recall under at least one cue and papers it never
claimed, and compare its accuracy from
[Table 3](#S4.T3 "In 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
on the two groups
([Table D.2](#A4.T2 "In Does remembering a paper help? ‣ Appendix D Do Frontier Models Memorize the Test Decisions? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
Recognized papers are no easier on either dataset (permutation $`p=.28`$
and $`.88`$), including on ICLR ’25, the only ICLR year inside its
cutoff, and accuracy does not rise with the number of cues under which a
paper is recognized. Papers whose recalled decision happened to be
correct do score higher, but this is circular, since those are the
papers where the model’s impression already matched the outcome.

We conclude that GPT-5.5 recognizes a substantial fraction of our test
papers but does not retrieve their decisions, and that its baseline
accuracy in
[Table 3](#S4.T3 "In 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
is not explained by memorization.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
````
