````math
## Appendix F Training Variations

### F.1 Evaluation and Training Prior Investigation

The main text reports balanced test metrics because our decision
objective is Acc. This is compatible with natural-rate reporting when
balanced and natural samples come from the same curated domain
distribution. The accept and reject recalls estimated on a balanced test
can be reweighted by the natural accept prior.
[Table F.1](#A6.T1 "In F.1 Evaluation and Training Prior Investigation ‣ Appendix F Training Variations ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
checks this directly for matched ICLR and arXiv 7B text and vision
predictors. Across all four cells, the empirical natural-rate accuracy
lands within a few percentage points of the prior-extrapolated value, so
the balanced test keeps the metric aligned with the objective.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Domain | Predictor | Balanced Acc | Extrapolated natural | Empirical natural | $`\boldsymbol{\Delta}`$ |
| ICLR | Vision | 68.3 | 68.0 | 65.6 | -2.4 |
| ICLR | Text | 66.0 | 67.2 | 64.1 | -3.1 |
| arXiv | Vision | 73.4 | 74.2 | 75.1 | +1.0 |
| arXiv | Text | 71.3 | 71.7 | 72.0 | +0.3 |

Table F.1: Balanced-to-natural extrapolation. For matched
ICLR$`\rightarrow`$ICLR and arXiv$`\rightarrow`$arXiv diagnostics,
balanced-test accept and reject recalls are converted to raw accuracy
under the natural test prior. $`\Delta`$ is empirical natural-prior
accuracy minus this extrapolated value.

The training-prior diagnostic in
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.1 Datasets ‣ Section 3 PaperScorer: Dataset and Methods ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
uses validation thresholds only to reveal class-prior bias. All headline
PaperScorer results use native decisions unless stated otherwise (e.g.,
calibration).

### F.2 Ablating Training Distribution and Paper Representation

We explored two families of training ablations on ICLR to improve
decision accuracy. The first filtered training papers to high-quality
accepts and rejects by reviewer rating, dropping borderline papers. The
second tested additional context suffixes such as paper statistics,
agent-generated reviews, and vision-text fusion to support the decision
objective. Both are summarized in
[Table F.2](#A6.T2 "In F.2 Ablating Training Distribution and Paper Representation ‣ Appendix F Training Variations ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?").

Table
[F.2](#A6.T2 "Table F.2 ‣ F.2 Ablating Training Distribution and Paper Representation ‣ Appendix F Training Variations ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")a
shows that training only on pre-’26 data does not transfer well to ’26.
To improve the quality of the corpus, we tried to filter out borderline
cases via *Rating-Agreeing*, which keeps only accepts in $`[0.6,1]`$ and
rejects in $`[0,0.4]`$ by percentile rating. It helps on ’25, but once
’26 is included, it does not improve either modality noticeably. Table
[F.2](#A6.T2 "Table F.2 ‣ F.2 Ablating Training Distribution and Paper Representation ‣ Appendix F Training Variations ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")b
explains why: ’26 is fundamentally a different distribution, since the
rebuttal process was cut short, author-reviewer discussion was not
allowed, and reviewers could not raise scores, yielding the smallest
accept-reject gap. Table
[F.2](#A6.T2 "Table F.2 ‣ F.2 Ablating Training Distribution and Paper Representation ‣ Appendix F Training Variations ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")c
shows that additional context helps text, especially for ’26 transfer,
but harms vision, our strongest model. We therefore train on the
simplest paper-only pool, ’20–’23, ’25–’26^(∗), which gives the
strongest vision results without sacrificing text performance.

Table F.2: Data mixture breakdown. We report fixed-cost data and context
ablations, with underlined rows as bases and following rows as deltas.
Rating-agreeing data helps ’25 but not the final ’26-oriented setup; ’26
has the smallest accept-reject rating gap; and extra feature/review
context helps text modestly but not the strongest vision model.

We also tested several fixed-compute design choices beyond the
paper-only input. As Table
[F.2](#A6.T2 "Table F.2 ‣ F.2 Ablating Training Distribution and Paper Representation ‣ Appendix F Training Variations ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")c
shows, suffixing text with paper statistics or agent-generated
Qwen/Gemini reviews can help text modestly, especially on ’26, but none
of these additions improves the strongest vision model. The same is true
for other fixed-cost variants such as suffixing text with full vision,
vision with full text, or prepending 1k \<think\> tokens. None of these
design choices consistently improves performance, so we simply use paper
$`\to`$ decision prediction.

Paper statistics features. We appended structured metadata such as page
count, number of references, inline math count, cross-reference density,
and other surface-level features to each training sample. While these
features are individually predictive, adding them to the SFT prompt did
not improve over the paper-only baseline, suggesting that the language
model already captures these signals implicitly from the paper text.

Thinking tokens. Inspired by chain-of-thought prompting, we prepended
dummy reasoning tokens before the decision token during SFT, allowing
the model additional computation before committing to a prediction. This
did not improve accuracy, consistent with our finding that the decision
task benefits more from pattern recognition over the full paper than
from explicit multi-step reasoning.

Multimodal fusion. We tested providing both the full extracted text and
screenshots of all pages simultaneously (text + vision), as well as the
reverse (vision + text). Neither configuration outperformed the
single-modality baselines, likely because the two representations are
largely redundant for the decision task, and the additional context
length increases noise without adding a complementary signal.

Synthetic review augmentation. Appending model-generated reviews
(Qwen3.5-122B-A10B or Gemini-2.5-Flash) to training prompts added
$`{\sim}1.8`$k–$`4.8`$k tokens per sample. These reviews occasionally
helped on ICLR ’25 but hurt on ICLR ’26, suggesting that review language
is more year-specific than paper content and does not transfer reliably.

### F.3 Reverse-Order Ablation

To test whether SFT models rely on positional shortcuts, we reversed the
paper order while keeping labels fixed — text examples reverse section
blocks, and vision examples reverse page order. Training and evaluating
in the same reversed condition only loses about 1–1.3% relative to the
forward baseline, and forward-trained checkpoints remain usable on
reversed validation inputs (Table
[F.3](#A6.T3 "Table F.3 ‣ F.3 Reverse-Order Ablation ‣ Appendix F Training Variations ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
This suggests the models are not merely keying on early-section or
early-page cues; vision is especially order-invariant.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Training | Evaluation | Accuracy | n |
| Matched training and evaluation order |  |  |  |
| Forward (vision) | Forward | 68.4% | 2,498 |
| Reversed (vision) | Reversed | 67.2% | 2,498 |
| Forward (text) | Forward | 67.0% | 2,495 |
| Reversed (text) | Reversed | 65.7% | 2,495 |
| Forward-trained checkpoints, reversed-order evaluation |  |  |  |
| Forward (vision) | Reversed | 66.1% | 1,253 |
| Forward (text) | Reversed | 64.9% | 1,252 |

Table F.3: Reverse-order ablation. Reversing text section blocks or
vision page order during training and evaluation costs only
$`1`$–$`1.3`$ points of accuracy. Forward-trained checkpoints also stay
close to their forward accuracy when evaluated on reversed inputs,
indicating that vision in particular is largely order-invariant.

## Appendix G Cross-Source Generalization

How does a model trained on one source behave on the other? We evaluate
the ICLR-trained and arXiv-trained 7B vision models on each source’s
test set and on arXiv-ICLR, the ICLR subset of arXiv (Table
[G.1](#A7.T1 "Table G.1 ‣ Appendix G Cross-Source Generalization ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Train $`\to`$ test (7B vision) | $`R_{A}`$ | $`R_{R}`$ | Acc | $`n`$ |
| *Generalizes: accept and reject recall stay balanced* |  |  |  |  |
| ICLR $`\to`$ ICLR | 69.2 | 67.4 | 68.3 | 1670 |
| ICLR $`\to`$ arXiv-ICLR | 78.3 | 69.5 | 73.9 | 105 |
| *Reject-predictive off-domain: $`R_{R}`$ holds, $`R_{A}`$ collapses* |  |  |  |  |
| arXiv $`\to`$ ICLR | 52.5 | 68.9 | 60.7 | 1670 |
| ICLR $`\to`$ arXiv (all) | 50.1 | 78.2 | 64.2 | 1414 |

Table G.1: Cross-source generalization (7B vision). Accept recall
($`R_{A}`$), reject recall ($`R_{R}`$), and accuracy (Acc), in %, over
$`n`$ test papers. ICLR training reaches arXiv-ICLR without loss. But
faced with the other source’s full set, a model still flags its rejects
and recovers only about half of its accepts.

The ICLR-trained model transfers to arXiv-ICLR with no measurable loss
(Table
[G.1](#A7.T1 "Table G.1 ‣ Appendix G Cross-Source Generalization ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
With only $`105`$ papers, though, its accuracy there has a $`95\%`$
confidence interval that overlaps its in-domain accuracy, so we read
this as equal performance, not a real gain. A much larger effect appears
when either model is run on the full distribution of the other source.
Both become reject-predictive, recovering only about half of the true
accepts, so each defaults to rejection on papers that look unfamiliar.

This is not a threshold problem. We retuned the accept/reject threshold
on a small labeled sample from the target source, and it only swapped
the error. Accepts then rose above $`88\%`$ while rejects fell below
$`40\%`$, and accuracy stayed flat. Even the best threshold chosen
directly on the test labels barely changed it. The model’s ranking of
papers, not the threshold, is what fails under the shift.

### H.1 Prompts

In this section we denote the prompts and decoding settings used during
prompting, SFT, and RL. We omit the paper body from the prompts for
brevity.

#### H.1.1 Base Open-Source Prompting

No Reasoning Prompt. Open-source Qwen and SFT runs share a minimal
answer-only prompt. The ICLR variant tells the model that ICLR accepts
around 30%, while the arXiv variant uses venue-generic wording because
the source-derived dataset spans multiple ML venues. For cross-source
evaluation, the wording follows the target dataset rather than the
training source.

\[System\]You are an expert academic reviewer tasked with evaluating
research papers.\[User --- ICLR\]I am giving you a paper. I want to
predict its acceptance outcome at ICLR. - Your answer will either be:
\boxed{Accept} or \boxed{Reject} - Note: ICLR generally has a ˜30%
acceptance rate\[User --- arXiv\]I am giving you a paper submitted to a
top machine-learning venue. Predictits acceptance outcome. - Your answer
will either be: \boxed{Accept} or \boxed{Reject} - Note: typical
top-tier ML venues have ˜25-30% acceptance rates

Reasoning Prompt. Reasoning prompts move the instruction into the system
turn and leave the user turn as the paper body. The full ICLR variant is
shown below. The arXiv variant replaces the first sentence with the
venue-generic top-ML wording. Vision reasoning prompts add that the
paper is provided as Markdown text plus screenshots of each page, and
ask the model to inspect page layouts.

\[System\]You are an expert academic reviewer for the ICLR conference,
predicting whether apaper will be accepted or rejected. ICLR generally
has a ˜30% acceptance rate.Your response must include two parts:1.
\*\*Reasoning\*\*: A detailed, free-flowing chain of thought enclosed
in‘\<think\>‘ and ‘\</think\>‘ tags.2. \*\*Final Answer\*\*: A single
boxed verdict enclosed in ‘\<answer\>‘ and‘\</answer\>‘ tags.\* The
reasoning should resemble a stream of consciousness: explore, test
hypotheses, backtrack if necessary, reflect, and refine.\* Use reasoning
strategies such as planning, exploration, evaluation, and reflection.\*
The answer section must be enclosed in ‘\<answer\>‘ and ‘\</answer\>‘
tags.\* The answer is exactly ‘\boxed{Accept}‘ or ‘\boxed{Reject}‘, with
no other text.\[User\]\<paper body as Markdown; vision variant also
attaches per-page screenshots\>

#### H.1.2 Frontier Model Prompting

Frontier Reasoning Prompt. Frontier Gemini and GPT models
(Gemini-3.1-Pro and GPT-5.5) use a single venue-generic
rating-plus-decision prompt for both ICLR and arXiv. We chose this
prompt after finding no consistent gain from separate ICLR- and
arXiv-specific variants. In practice, the venue is usually recoverable
from the paper content and formatting.

\[System\]You are an expert academic ML researcher and reviewer tasked
with evaluatingresearch papers. I am giving you a paper submitted to a
top machine-learning venue.Predict a rating from 1-10 and the paper’s
acceptance outcome. - Your answer will be of the form:
\boxed{rating,decision} where rating is an integer in \[1,10\] and
decision is either {Accept, Reject} - Note: typical top-tier ML venues
have ˜25-30% acceptance rates\[User\]\<paper body as Markdown; vision
variant also attaches per-page screenshots\>We use the generated rating
as the score, with a higher rating indicating a higher predicted
probability of acceptance, and the generated decision as the hard label.
In our main results we additionally calibrate the model’s decision using
its rating and accuracy performance on the held-out validation set,
which generally improves performance.

Frontier Reasoning Agent Workspace. Coding-agent baselines use the same
Frontier Reasoning Prompt above (carried in AGENTS.override.md), but
place each paper in a self-contained workspace that the agent can
inspect with normal file and image tools. The paper body is stripped
into paper.md, rendered pages are copied into images/, and the final
answer must be written to PREDICTIONS.json. Both Codex (GPT-5.5) and
Claude Code (Sonnet-4.6) run with high reasoning effort, no web tools,
and a validator that rejects malformed outputs before grading.

agent_workspaces/\<sample\>/\<domain\>/\<paper_id\>/\|--
AGENTS.override.md \# rating + accept/reject instruction\|-- CLAUDE.md
-\> AGENTS.override.md\|-- id.txt \# paper identifier\|-- paper.md \#
stripped markdown paper body\|-- images/\| \|-- page_1.png\| \|--
page_2.png\| ‘-- ...\|-- main.py \# calls the schema validator‘--
results/ \|-- codex/ \| \|-- PREDICTIONS.json \| ‘-- session.jsonl ‘--
claude/ \|-- PREDICTIONS.json ‘-- session.jsonlGrading joins each valid
PREDICTIONS.json with the held-out ground-truth manifest and reports
accuracy, accept/reject recall, and rating correlation. The workspace
tree is intentionally one paper at a time, matching the single-shot API
setup while letting the agent choose whether to read markdown, rendered
pages, or both modalities together.

### H.2 Frontier Model Reasoning Usage

[Table H.2](#A8.T2 "In H.2 Frontier Model Reasoning Usage ‣ Appendix H Prompting and Extended Experiments ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
reports reasoning-token usage across the four ICLR/arXiv text/vision
evaluation cells. Both frontier models spend a substantial amount of
reasoning compute per paper. On text inputs, median reasoning tokens
land between $`1.3`$k and $`2.3`$k per paper, and on vision inputs
between $`1.5`$k and $`2.1`$k. P95 reasoning length stretches to
$`3.6`$k–$`4.7`$k, so a non-trivial tail of papers triggers $`2\times`$
or more compute than the median. GPT-5.5 has a lower median than
Gemini-3.1-Pro at every cell, but its tail is just as heavy: its P95
sits at $`3.6`$k–$`4.5`$k against Gemini-3.1-Pro’s $`4.1`$k–$`4.7`$k,
and its P95-to-median ratio is the larger of the two, so its compute
varies more from paper to paper. ICLR cells consistently use more
reasoning than the matched arXiv cells (e.g. Gemini-3.1-Pro at
$`2{,}085`$ vision-median tokens on ICLR vs $`1{,}825`$ on arXiv),
suggesting that ICLR papers either look harder or hit prompts that
elicit more deliberation.

### H.3 Correcting Model Biases with Prompting

Base open-source models we tested predict acceptance for almost every
paper. Out of the box, Qwen2.5-7B with a minimal freeform-boxed prompt
accepts more than $`99\%`$ of papers
([Table 3(a)](#A8.T3.st1 "In Table H.3 ‣ H.3 Correcting Model Biases with Prompting ‣ Appendix H Prompting and Extended Experiments ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"),
Freeform Boxed Standard: $`R_{A}=99.4`$, $`R_{R}=0.9`$). We therefore
tested a range of prompt corrections, few-shot conditioning, and
multi-step peer-review emulation across two open-source models
(Qwen2.5-7B text and vision, all $`2{,}495`$ ICLR test papers) and a
cheap frontier model (Gemini-2.5-Flash text and vision, a $`500`$-paper
stratified subset). All numbers are averages across ’25 and ’26.

Prompt variants. We compare four prompt formats. *Freeform Boxed*
requests a boxed Accept/Reject answer with no structure. *Structured
JSON* requests a full review schema (summary, strengths, weaknesses,
score, decision). *Fewshot 1A-1R* prepends one accept and one reject
calibration example. *Fewshot 0A-2R* uses two reject examples. Each
format can be paired with a *Critical* modifier (an explicit instruction
to be wary of overstated claims and to prefer rejection when uncertain).
Multi-turn variants include *Majority voting* over 5 generations,
*Meta-Review* (the Sequential Refinement of [Madaan et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib29)), and *PDR Boxed* (a single-generation
Parallel-Distill-Reflect prompt that runs an Advocate, Critic, and
Calibrator inside one rollout).

Critical variant. Appending a single “be critical, prefer rejection when
uncertain” instruction is not enough to stop the model from predicting
acceptance for nearly every paper. On Qwen2.5-7B text, Freeform Boxed
Critical only nudges reject recall from $`0.9\%`$ to $`4.3\%`$.
Switching to Structured JSON (a full review schema with strengths,
weaknesses, score, and decision fields) with the Critical modifier
produces a larger swing ($`R_{R}=31.8\%`$ for text, $`32.1\%`$ for
vision), but accuracy stays at chance ($`\sim`$$`50\%`$).
Gemini-2.5-Flash predicts acceptance less often to begin with
($`R_{A}=70.2\%`$ for text under Freeform Boxed Standard), and adding
Critical overshoots, so that it predicts rejection too often
($`R_{R}=75.7\%`$ for text, $`67.0\%`$ for vision) without changing
accuracy. Across both model families, prompting can rebalance
accept/reject recall but cannot lift accuracy above the majority
baseline.

Multi-step peer-review emulation. Multi-turn variants that simulate a
reviewer panel, including 5-generation Majority voting, Sequential
Refinement Meta-Review ([Madaan et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)), and the
single-generation Parallel-Distill-Reflect (PDR) prompt with Advocate,
Critic, and Calibrator roles, move recall but not accuracy. Majority
voting on Freeform Critical preserves Qwen’s single-turn tendency to
accept nearly everything ($`R_{A}=97.3`$, $`R_{R}=4.9`$). Few-shot 1A-1R
Standard with Majority voting partially rebalances ($`R_{A}=47.5`$,
$`R_{R}=59.1`$), and PDR Boxed reaches $`R_{A}=65.1`$, $`R_{R}=35.2`$.
None of these multi-turn prompts breaks the $`\sim`$$`50\%`$ ceiling on
ICLR, consistent with our main-text observation that base-model
prompting alone does not recover the decision signal that SFT later
captures from the same backbones.

## Appendix I SFT and RL Method Details

### I.1 SFT

SFT uses cosine decay with 5 warmup steps, context length 24,480 tokens,
and greedy evaluation. The strongest text configuration uses batch size
32 with a learning rate of $`10^{-6}`$. The strongest vision
configuration uses batch size 16 with the same learning rate. We sweep
ICLR and arXiv training sources, 50/50 versus natural-rate class priors,
data scale, text versus screenshot inputs, text+vision variants, and
suffixes containing structured paper statistics or Qwen/Gemini-generated
reviews. For vision efficiency, we also test the panel setup in Table
[4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"),
which tiles ten pages into one 2380$`\times`$1512 image. Unless a row is
explicitly marked otherwise, 3B SFT runs train for 4 epochs and 7B/14B
SFT runs train for 2 epochs.

Figure I.1: RL training curves: strict accuracy and per-class recall.
*Left:* strict-accuracy training estimate (EMA-smoothed; raw curve in
faint background) and held-out eval accuracy on 1,667 ’25/’26 papers.
The training estimate is inverted from the graded reward via
$`\mathrm{acc}\approx(r-0.2\cdot b)/(1-0.2\cdot b)`$ where the
boxed-rate $`b\approx 1.0`$ on every eval. *Right:* per-class accept
($`R_{A}`$, circles, solid) and reject ($`R_{R}`$, squares, dashed)
recall on the same eval set. Both policies show graded reward improving
during training, but their pre-existing accept bias is preserved and
tightens further as RL continues.

### I.2 RL

We train two single-turn GRPO policies following DeepSeek-R1 ([Guo et
al., 2025](#bib.bib16)), one text and one vision-language, on ICLR. Both
apply the reasoning prompt variant from [Appendix
H.1](#A8.SS1 "H.1 Prompts ‣ Appendix H Prompting and Extended Experiments ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
on the base Qwen2.5-7B (text) and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (vision)
models, and use the composite accuracy-plus-format reward described in
the main text.
[Figure I.1](#A9.F1 "In I.1 SFT ‣ Appendix I SFT and RL Method Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
shows training trajectories through step $`100`$ on a 1,667-paper
held-out ’25/’26 ICLR test set. Both policies show graded reward
climbing during training, but the per-class recall panel exposes that
the underlying accept/reject mix barely shifts. As the models learn to
satisfy the format reward, their pre-existing accept bias is preserved
and even tightens further during RL. Neither policy surpasses the
strongest SFT model from the main text. The graded reward partially
hides the swing because every well-formed prediction already earns a
$`0.2`$ format floor before the decision term contributes anything.

Settings. The text RL policy uses a learning rate of
$`1.2\times 10^{-6}`$ with constant warmup over 4 steps, max gradient
norm $`0.5`$, train batch size $`256`$, policy mini-batch size $`128`$,
micro-batch size $`2`$ per GPU, one epoch, $`8`$ rollouts per prompt,
max response length $`4096`$, and max prompt length $`25{,}480`$. The
vision RL policy uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct with a learning rate of
$`10^{-6}`$, train batch size $`64`$, PPO mini-batch size $`32`$,
micro-batch size $`2`$ per GPU, one epoch, $`8`$ rollouts per prompt,
max response length $`2046`$, and max prompt length $`24{,}480`$. Each
paper is represented by roughly $`10`$ PNG screenshots plus text.

### I.3 Calibration Details

Modern neural networks are often poorly calibrated, producing confidence
estimates that do not reflect true correctness probabilities ([Guo et
al., 2017](#bib.bib15)). We apply post-hoc temperature scaling to our
SFT models and to Jev, with a base-rate term so the probabilities hold
at a venue’s real acceptance rate.

Expected calibration error. Following [Guo et al. (2017)](#bib.bib15),
we first convert each prediction into confidence in the chosen decision:
$`c_{i}=p_{i}`$ when $`\hat{z}_{i}{=}1`$ and $`c_{i}=1-p_{i}`$ when
$`\hat{z}_{i}{=}0`$. We partition these confidences into $`M`$
equal-width bins $`B_{1},\ldots,B_{M}`$ and define the *expected
calibration error* (ECE) as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{|B_{m}|}{n}\left|\mathrm{acc}(B_{m})-\mathrm{conf}(B_{m})\right|,
``` |  | (1) |

where
$`\mathrm{acc}(B_{m})=|B_{m}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_{m}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{z}_{i}=z_{i}]`$
is the empirical accuracy and
$`\mathrm{conf}(B_{m})=|B_{m}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_{m}}c_{i}`$ is the mean
confidence in that bin. ECE is therefore the average discrepancy between
how confident the model is and how often it is correct; a perfectly
calibrated model has $`\mathrm{ECE}=0`$.

Raw calibration. Before scaling, the text models are close to
calibrated, with ECE $`0.027`$ on ICLR and $`0.043`$ on arXiv (balanced
test). The vision models are overconfident, with ECE $`0.049`$ and
$`0.069`$: their confidence exceeds their accuracy.

Temperature scaling with a base-rate term. Temperature scaling uses a
single parameter $`\tau>0`$. From the decision-token log-probabilities
we take the accept log-odds
$`\ell=\log P(\text{Accept})-\log P(\text{Reject})`$. Our models are
trained on a 50/50 mix, so $`\ell`$ measures the evidence under a
balanced prior. To score papers at acceptance rate $`\pi`$ we add the
prior log-odds and rescale:

|     |                                                               |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       p_{\mathrm{cal}}=\sigma\big(\ell/\tau+\log(\pi/(1-\pi))\big),
       ```                                                            |     | (2) |

where $`\sigma`$ is the sigmoid function. $`\tau>1`$ softens
overconfident predictions and $`\tau<1`$ sharpens them. We fit $`\tau`$
by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL) on the natural-rate
validation split, with $`\pi`$ set to that split’s acceptance rate
($`31\%`$ for ICLR, $`23\%`$ for arXiv), so the shift absorbs the base
rate and $`\tau`$ only sets how sharp the probabilities are. On a
balanced set $`\pi=0.5`$ and the shift vanishes. Jev’s scores already
sit near the real acceptance rate, so we fit its $`\tau`$ without the
shift and, on balanced sets, subtract $`\log(\pi/(1-\pi))`$ instead.
Since $`p_{\mathrm{cal}}\geq\pi`$ exactly when $`\ell\geq 0`$, neither
$`\tau`$ nor the shift ever changes a decision.

We do not minimize ECE directly because (i) the binning operation is
non-differentiable, (ii) ECE is sensitive to the number of bins, and
(iii) NLL is a strictly proper scoring rule whose global optimum is
achieved if and only if predicted probabilities equal true
probabilities. ECE, by contrast, can be zero even with poorly separated
and rank-uninformative predictions.

Calibration at the real acceptance rate. On a natural-rate set we
measure the calibration of the acceptance probability itself: we bin
papers by $`p_{\mathrm{cal}}`$ into ten equal-width bins on $`[0,1]`$
and take the size-weighted gap between each bin’s mean
$`p_{\mathrm{cal}}`$ and the fraction of its papers actually accepted.
[Table I.1](#A9.T1 "In I.3 Calibration Details ‣ Appendix I SFT and RL Method Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
and Figure
[I.2](#A9.F2 "Figure I.2 ‣ I.3 Calibration Details ‣ Appendix I SFT and RL Method Details ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
evaluate the shift on the natural-rate test sets. Without it, the
probabilities stay centered for a 50/50 world and overstate acceptance
(ECE $`.13`$–$`.15`$). With it, ECE falls to $`.023`$–$`.042`$ for
PaperScorer. At this rate an ICLR Accept call by PaperScorer-Vision is
right $`47\%`$ of the time and a Reject call $`82\%`$ ($`56\%`$ and
$`91\%`$ on arXiv). The shifted probabilities slightly understate
acceptance: their mean is $`29.3\%`$ where $`31.3\%`$ of ICLR papers are
accepted, and $`21.8\%`$ where $`24.8\%`$ of arXiv papers are.

Robustness. Fitting $`\tau`$ on a balanced validation split instead, and
adding the same shift, gives similar results (ECE $`.030`$–$`.049`$). A
two-parameter Platt fit ([Platt, 1999](#bib.bib35)), $`\sigma(a\ell+b)`$
on the natural-rate split, is slightly better still
($`0.017`$–$`0.031`$) and also calibrates Jev ($`0.018`$–$`0.021`$).
Jev’s calibrated probabilities, however, never exceed about $`60\%`$, so
unlike PaperScorer it cannot single out likely accepts.

Caveats. The arXiv model’s $`\pi`$ is a mix of venue rates (about
$`23\%`$); a single venue’s rate can be plugged in as $`\pi`$. arXiv
rejects are inferred, never matched to a proceedings entry, rather than
confirmed.

|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\tau`$ |  | Balanced test ECE |  | Natural-rate test ECE of $`p_{\mathrm{cal}}`$ |  |  |  |
| Source | Model | Ours | Bal. val | Raw | Ours | No shift | Ours | Bal.-val $`\tau`$ | Platt |

### I.4 Hardware Details

All SFT and RL experiments reported in the paper run on a single node
with $`4\times`$ NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Per-eval inference for the held-out
checkpoints uses the same node.

## Appendix J Statistical Uncertainty

For uncertainty estimates, we use paired bootstrap resampling so each
resample compares models on the same papers. We resample paper IDs
10,000 times with replacement and recompute Acc and AUC on each
resample.
[Table J.1](#A10.T1 "In Appendix J Statistical Uncertainty ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
reports percentile 95% two-sided CIs for the four headline
PaperScorer-Vision comparisons. On ICLR, the Acc gap against
Gemini-3.1-Pro is $`+3.8\%`$ with CI $`[+0.4,+7.3]`$, and the AUC gap
against GPT-5.5 is $`+.066`$ with CI $`[+.034,+.098]`$. On arXiv, the
Acc gap against Gemini-3.1-Pro is $`+8.7\%`$ (CI $`[+4.5,+12.7]`$) and
the AUC gap against GPT-5.5 is $`+.097`$ (CI $`[+.061,+.135]`$). Since
our claim is directional, we test it one-sided; all four are significant
($`p\leq.014`$). The same holds for every large frontier configuration:
against Gemini-3.1-Pro and GPT-5.5 with either text or vision input,
with decisions thresholded as in Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"),
the one-sided $`p`$ is below $`.05`$ for both Acc and AUC on both
datasets (largest $`p=.040`$, Acc against GPT-5.5 with text input on
ICLR).

Correlative analysis. Binary accept/reject training yields a continuous
score that also tracks reviewer ratings and later citations. On ICLR,
PaperScorer-Vision has the strongest PaperScorer rating alignment
($`\rho_{R}=+.48`$), while PaperScorer-Text at 14B is strongest within
PaperScorer for ’25 citation alignment ($`\rho_{C}=+.31`$). On arXiv,
reviewer ratings and citations are available for fewer papers than
decisions are, so we treat them as diagnostics and leave them out of the
headline comparisons. On ICLR ’25, the one slice with both full reviewer
ratings and citations ($`n=678`$), PaperScorer-Vision’s
$`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ tracks later citations about as well as the
human review score ($`\rho\approx.25`$ vs. $`.26`$), and accepted papers
outcite rejected ones (citation AUC $`.64`$). We cannot run this check
on arXiv, whose citations come only from proceedings-matched accepts,
leaving too few rejected papers to compare.

Frontier model repeatability. We repeated a subset of the frontier-model
inference calls on the same held-out arXiv-text papers to estimate
run-to-run noise. GPT-5.4 is almost deterministic under the same prompt,
while Gemini-3.1-Pro has meaningful stochasticity. Decision agreement is
89.4% and the second pass is 4.5% lower on the same papers (Table
[J.3](#A10.T3 "Table J.3 ‣ Appendix J Statistical Uncertainty ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
We therefore treat GPT-5.4 point estimates as stable, while Gemini
estimates should be read with several points of implicit run noise
unless repeated passes are averaged. This repeatability audit was run on
GPT-5.4, the frontier model used before we re-ran the main GPT baseline
on GPT-5.5; we did not separately re-audit GPT-5.5’s run-to-run noise.

## Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems

PaperScorer produces a ranking signal that is empirically proven: its
high AUC and rating correlation show that the score ranks accepted
papers above rejected ones and agrees with reviewer ratings, and
temperature scaling makes that score calibrated after the fact. This
invites two applications where a calibrated estimate of acceptance
probability matters. In literature retrieval, we want to surface work
likely to be accepted among topically similar candidates. In agentic
reviewing, a generated critique relies on a well-calibrated prior over
the final decision. We study both settings below.

Figure K.1: LitSearch reranking. We evaluate Recall@K on 148 hard
LitSearch queries whose gold papers are missed by BM25 at K=5, using
each retriever’s top-200 candidates. Labels show the Recall@K gain from
adding PaperScorer-Vision.

### K.1 Ranking Scientific Literature for Retrieval

Scientific search systems must retrieve a target paper from many
plausible topical matches. LitSearch ([Ajith et al., 2024](#bib.bib3))
captures this setting with natural-language literature queries paired
with one or more gold cited papers. We evaluate the subset linked to our
arXiv pool: 478 queries have at least one gold arXiv paper, and 250 have
all gold arXiv IDs inside the PaperScorer arXiv corpus. To isolate the
regime where reranking matters, we use the 148 hard queries for which
BM25 has zero Recall@5, covering 150 gold papers.

We use PaperScorer as a query-independent reranker based on its
estimated acceptance probability. For each hard query, BM25 and
Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B ([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib53)) first retrieve
their own top-200 candidate papers. We then score each candidate once
with arXiv-trained PaperScorer-Vision (7B checkpoint, matching the main
results); the 3B checkpoint (not shown) reranks almost as well, within a
few percent at every $`K`$, consistent with our finding that decision
accuracy is largely insensitive to model scale
([Section 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
Let $`s(q,d)`$ be the retriever score for candidate $`d`$ under query
$`q`$, let $`z(\cdot)`$ denote $`z`$-normalization within the query’s
candidate list, and let $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}(d)`$ be the PaperScorer
acceptance score. We rank candidates by a fixed blend of the two, with
the weight on $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ chosen on a held-out validation
split of queries:

|     |                                             |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       0.3\,z(s(q,d))+0.7\,p_{\mathrm{accept}}(d).
       ```                                          |     |

Retrieval supplies the topical neighborhood, while PaperScorer-Vision
reorders candidates by their estimated acceptance probability.
[Figure K.1](#A11.F1 "In Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
shows that this helps both retrievers: whether candidates come from
sparse BM25 or a dense Qwen embedding, reranking pulls more of the gold
cited papers toward the top of the list. The gain is largest near the
top, where retrieval has already gathered topically similar work and the
only open question is which paper is more likely to be accepted. Deeper
down, where topical relevance still does most of the sorting, the prior
adds little, so PaperScorer-Vision acts as a prior on acceptance layered
on retrieval, not a substitute for it.

### K.2 Grounding Agentic Reviewers

Prior work shows that LLM reviews can yield actionable suggestions for
improving papers ([Thakkar et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)), but our
prompt-tuning results
([Section 4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"))
suggest that the predicted decisions poorly track ground-truth outcomes.
As noted in
[Section 2](#S2 "Section 2 Problem Formulation ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?"),
papers $`X`$ are transformed into reviews $`R`$ before reaching a
decision $`Z`$, so the joint distribution over reviews and decisions
factors as $`p(R,Z\mid X)`$. While the autoregressive flow places the
review before the decision, now that we have built a shortcut that
predicts the decision without the review, we can ask whether we can
generate more *decision-calibrated* reviews by rearranging the joint:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(R,Z\mid X)=p(Z\mid R,X)\,p(R\mid X)\;\Longrightarrow\;\overbrace{p(R\mid Z,X)}^{\text{Frontier Model}}\,\overbrace{p(Z\mid X)}^{\text{{\color[rgb]{0.1836,0.3281,0.5898}\textbf{PaperScorer}}{}}}.
``` |  |

Both factorizations are valid. Conceptually, if our conjecture is
correct — that much of the decision is determined by overall
presentation quality — then reviews may serve as a means-to-an-end to
justify the reviewer’s initial reaction. This follows from psychology
research on human decision-making, whereby we often rely on initial
judgments and post-hoc rationalization more than we consciously
attribute ([Nisbett and Wilson, 1977](#bib.bib31); [Kunda,
1990](#bib.bib24); [Haidt, 2001](#bib.bib17)), with low-level feelings
of “goodness” or “badness” driving longer-form judgments and reasoning
([Slovic et al., 2007](#bib.bib38)).

We therefore ask whether conditioning frontier coding agents on the
PaperScorer signal can (1) improve their decision-prediction and (2)
improve their generated reviews’ alignment with human reviews. We use
PaperScorer-Vision as the calibrated prior, and let Claude Code write
the review.

|                       |          |      |      |                 |       |       |       |       |
|-----------------------|----------|------|------|-----------------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
|                       | Acc. (%) |      |      | Alignment (1–5) |       |       |       |       |
|  Method               | ’25      | ’26  | All  | Cn.             | Wk.   | Nov.  | Ql.   | Mean  |
|  PaperScorer-Vision   | 72.0     | 68.0 | 69.6 | –               | –     | –     | –     | –     |
|  Claude Code          | 57.5     | 66.7 | 63.0 | 4.96            | 4.08  | 3.98  | 4.11  | 4.28  |
|  +PaperScorer-Vision  | 70.5     | 70.7 | 70.6 | 4.87            | 4.23  | 4.10  | 4.14  | 4.33  |
|  $`\Delta`$           | +13.0    | +4.0 | +7.6 | -0.09           | +0.15 | +0.11 | +0.03 | +0.05 |

(a) Reviewer accuracy and human-review alignment. ‘Cn.’, ‘Wk.’, ‘Nov.’,
and ‘Ql.’ denote contribution, weakness, novel-concern, and
overall-quality alignment.

|             |      |      |      |      |         |      |
|-------------|------|------|------|------|---------|------|
|             | ’25  |      | ’26  |      | Overall |      |
| Transition  | %    | Acc. | %    | Acc. | %       | Acc. |
| No change   | 75.0 | 68.7 | 80.7 | 73.1 | 78.4    | 71.4 |
| A $`\to`$ R | 21.0 | 81.0 | 8.7  | 73.1 | 13.6    | 77.9 |

shift under the prior.

Table K.1: Decision-conditioned review generation. Claude Code is
evaluated on 500 ICLR papers under a 30/70 accept/reject split, with and
without the calibrated PaperScorer-Vision prior. Conditioning improves
accuracy from 63.0% to 70.6% and review alignment, with the prior
catching Claude’s remaining incorrect acceptance predictions.

We evaluate Claude Code (Sonnet-4.6) on 500 ICLR papers. The agent
receives PaperScorer-Vision’s decision, $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$, and
confidence bands, and can inspect text, rendered pages, and the
temporally filtered arXiv retrieval. It emits a schema-constrained
review and decision. Codex (GPT-5.5, medium reasoning) grades reviews
against human reviews (review generation and alignment grading prompts
in [Appendix
K.3](#A11.SS3 "K.3 Agentic Reviewer Prompts ‣ Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).

[Table 1(a)](#A11.T1.st1 "In Table K.1 ‣ K.2 Grounding Agentic Reviewers ‣ Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
shows that Claude alone *underperforms* PaperScorer-Vision, but adding
the calibrated prior improves overall accuracy from 63.0% to 70.6%,
surpassing both individually. This matches the factorization above.
PaperScorer-Vision anchors the decision while the reviewer supplies the
critique. The gain comes mainly from a 13.6% subset of papers flipping
Accept$`\to`$Reject at 77.9% accuracy
([Table 1(b)](#A11.T1.st2 "In Table K.1 ‣ K.2 Grounding Agentic Reviewers ‣ Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
Reject$`\to`$Accept flips are rarer and much less reliable. Although
Claude predicts rejection more often than acceptance on the balanced
evaluation
([Table 3](#S4.T3 "In 4.3 Main Results ‣ Section 4 Results ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
on this 30/70 subset its remaining incorrect acceptance predictions
dominate the correction signal, which the calibrated accept probability
catches by pulling those papers below the decision threshold the agent
then respects.

Conditioning on PaperScorer-Vision also improves alignment with human
reviews across every factor except contributions
([Table 1(a)](#A11.T1.st1 "In Table K.1 ‣ K.2 Grounding Agentic Reviewers ‣ Appendix K Applications to Scientific Systems ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
Because the prior corrects Claude’s accept-bias, the agent emits
weakness and novelty critiques at a higher rate, bringing the generated
review closer to the human ground truth. Contribution alignment was
already saturated under Claude alone, and is preserved under
conditioning.

### K.3 Agentic Reviewer Prompts

This subsection records the prompt scaffolding for the discussion
experiment. Claude Code (Sonnet-4.6) performs the review, while review
grading is performed by Codex (GPT-5.5) with medium reasoning.

Reviewer agent (no prior).

You are an ICLR reviewer. Review the paper with submission_id=\<SID\>.
STEPS: 1. Read the paper content from papers/\<SID\>/content.json 2.
Examine the page images listed in the content JSON under img_pages 3.
Write a structured ICLR review as JSON with all 11 fields: - decision:
"accept" or "reject" - rating: 0-10 - confidence: 1-5 - soundness: 1-4 -
presentation: 1-4 - contribution: 1-4 - summary: 2-3 sentence summary -
strengths: numbered list citing specific sections/figures/theorems -
weaknesses: numbered list citing specifics (no generic criticisms) -
questions: numbered list of questions for authors - missing_references:
prior work explicitly mentioned in the paper 4. Write the review JSON to
agent_reviews/\<SID\>.json using the Write tool. 5. Return ONLY "Done:
\<SID\>" -- do NOT return the full review text.

Reviewer agent (with PaperScorer-Vision prior).

You are an ICLR reviewer. Review the paper with submission_id=\<SID\>.
PAPERSCORER PRIOR: - Model prediction: \<accept\|reject\> - Model
confidence: \<0.xxx\> STEPS: 1. Read the paper content from
papers/\<SID\>/content.json 2. Examine the page images listed in the
content JSON under img_pages 3. Use the model prediction as a Bayesian
prior -- weight it by the confidence (high confidence -\> trust
strongly, low -\> use own judgment). 4. Write a structured ICLR review
as JSON with all 11 fields: - decision: "accept" or "reject" - rating:
0-10 - confidence: 1-5 - soundness: 1-4 - presentation: 1-4 -
contribution: 1-4 - summary: 2-3 sentence summary - strengths: numbered
list citing specific sections/figures/theorems - weaknesses: numbered
list citing specifics (no generic criticisms) - questions: numbered list
of questions for authors - missing_references: prior work explicitly
mentioned in the paper 5. Write the review JSON to
agent_reviews/\<SID\>.json using the Write tool. 6. Return ONLY "Done:
\<SID\>" -- do NOT return the full review text.

Judge prompt (Codex GPT-5.5, medium reasoning).

You are an expert meta-reviewer evaluating AI-generated paper reviews
against real ICLR human reviews and the Area Chair (AC) metareview. For
each paper you will see: - "human_reviews": individual ICLR reviewer
assessments - "metareview": the AC’s decision comment summarizing why
the paper was accepted/rejected - "agent_review": the AI-generated
review to evaluate EVALUATION PROTOCOL -- for EACH dimension, you
MUST: 1. QUOTE the relevant text from human reviews / metareview (use
"..." for excerpts) 2. QUOTE the relevant text from the agent review 3.
Explain your reasoning comparing the two 4. Assign a score 1-5
DIMENSIONS: 1. contribution_identification (1-5): What is the primary
contribution according to human reviewers? Did the agent identify the
same core contribution? - 5: Agent identifies the exact same core
contribution with similar framing - 4: Same contribution but framed
differently or missing a key aspect - 3: Related but focuses on a
secondary contribution instead of the primary one - 2: Vaguely related
to the actual contribution - 1: Completely different contribution
identified, or contribution not discussed 2. top_weakness_identification
(1-5): What is the \#1 weakness from human reviews? (The one most
reviewers agree on, or that the AC highlights in the metareview.) Did
the agent identify this specific weakness? - 5: Agent identifies the
same top weakness with comparable specificity and detail - 4: Identifies
the weakness but less precisely, or conflates it with other issues - 3:
Mentions the general area of concern but misses the specific technical
point - 2: Identifies only minor or tangential weaknesses, misses the
critical one entirely - 1: No meaningful overlap with human-identified
weaknesses 3. novel_concerns (1-5): List any concerns the agent raises
that are NOT present in human reviews or metareview. Are these valid and
substantive? - 5: Raises 2+ valid, substantive technical concerns that
humans missed - 4: Raises 1 valid substantive concern that humans
missed - 3: Raises concerns that are valid but minor, obvious, or not
very useful - 2: Novel concerns are mostly invalid, confused, or based
on misunderstanding the paper - 1: No novel concerns raised, or all
novel points are factually wrong 4. overall_review_quality (1-5):
Holistic quality considering: summary accuracy, weakness depth, strength
identification, constructiveness, specificity. - 5: Comparable to a good
human ICLR reviewer -- specific, evidence-based, actionable feedback -
4: Good review with paper-specific points but missing some depth or
nuance - 3: Adequate but generic -- observations could apply to many
papers in the area - 2: Superficial, repetitive, or contains factual
errors about the paper’s content - 1: Useless -- generic template text,
wrong paper content, or incoherent

## Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At?

### L.1 Section-Attention Map

Figure L.1: Section edits. (a) Later sections that receive more
attention also show a larger maximum observed change in
$`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ across four Git commits. (b) The most effective
edit type depends on the section: narrative helps Experiments and
Discussion, formalization helps Methodology, and nuance helps the
Introduction. Details in [Appendix
L.2](#A12.SS2 "L.2 Interpretability Details ‣ Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?").

|              |           |
|--------------|-----------|
| Section      | Attention |
| Discussion   | 37%       |
| Experiments  | 28%       |
| Methodology  | 15%       |
| Introduction | 9%        |
| Background   | 7%        |

Table L.1: Section attention.

We attribute the decision of PaperScorer to specific input features.
Using metadata from MinerU, we divide each paper into 5 sections:
Introduction, Background, Methodology, Experiments (including Results),
and Discussion (including Conclusion). Using the final decision token’s
last-layer attention as a descriptive map (described in [Appendix
L.2](#A12.SS2 "L.2 Interpretability Details ‣ Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")),
we observe a clear hierarchical preference as seen in [Table
L.1](#A12.T1 "Table L.1 ‣ L.1 Section-Attention Map ‣ Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?").
Generally, attention increases later in the paper. However, the
introduction is weighed more heavily than the background. We visualize
examples in [Figure
L.2](#A12.F2 "Figure L.2 ‣ L.2 Interpretability Details ‣ Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?").

Edit causality. To verify that this pattern represents the importance of
each section, we perform a causal experiment. We use Codex (gpt-5.5,
medium reasoning) to write independent, section-level edits to the
markdown paper copy of 30 accepted ’26 papers with low presentation
scores that PaperScorer-T scores as borderline (accept probability
between 0.45 and 0.50). Each Codex instance edits one section at a time,
allowing up to four sets of edits to be saved as Git commits, with
feedback from PaperScorer-T received after each commit. These changes
are constrained to presentation, framing, and style. We analyze the
$`\sim`$600 commits made. Details in [Appendix
L.2](#A12.SS2 "L.2 Interpretability Details ‣ Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?").

Our causal analysis matches the attention pattern: later sections,
especially Experiments and Discussion, show the largest maximum observed
changes in $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ in Figure
[L.1](#A12.F1 "Figure L.1 ‣ L.1 Section-Attention Map ‣ Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")a.
We find that the most effective edit type is section-dependent (Figure
[L.1](#A12.F1 "Figure L.1 ‣ L.1 Section-Attention Map ‣ Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")b).
Formalization helps most in methodology, narrative improvements help
most in the discussion and experiments, whereas substantiation in the
conclusion typically hurts acceptance probability. Notably, these edits
do not continuously increase $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$, suggesting that
PaperScorer-Text will only allow style edits to increase
$`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ to a certain threshold outside the 0.7
high-confidence region.

### L.2 Interpretability Details

Attention score definition. Following [Li et al. (2026)](#bib.bib25), we
use the last-layer attention of the final decision token to summarize
which paper tokens the model consults most strongly. Let
$`S=(x_{1},\dots,x_{T})`$ denote the full context, where the paper
occupies tokens $`x_{P+1},\dots,x_{T}`$. If $`\tau`$ is the generated
accept/reject token and $`\alpha_{\tau,i}`$ is the average attention
weight from $`\tau`$ to token $`i`$ across final-layer heads, then the
normalized paper-token attention score is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{\tau,i}=\frac{\alpha_{\tau,i}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\alpha_{\tau,j}},
``` |  |

where $`\mathcal{J}`$ indexes the paper tokens only. This gives a
probability distribution over the paper conditioned on the final
decision token. We aggregate these scores by section using text bbox
metadata from MinerU, then summarize the resulting distribution by
section medians in the main-text table.

![Refer to caption](2610.31791v1/attention_grid_raw_seed42.png)

Figure L.2: Full-paper attention heatmaps. Example attention overlay for
the SFT vision model. Regions highlighted in lighter colors receive more
of the final decision token’s last-layer attention mass. The model
concentrates most strongly on technical and evaluative material in the
latter half of the paper rather than on the opening framing alone.

Perturbation reasoning. The attention map is descriptive rather than
causal. A section may receive high last-layer attention because it
carries decisive evidence, but it could also inherit importance from
earlier-layer computation or from interactions across sections. We
therefore complement attention with direct perturbations: if editing one
section consistently changes PaperScorer-Text’s predicted acceptance
probability while all other sections remain fixed, that section is more
plausibly part of the model’s effective decision boundary.

Perturbation setup. We select 30 borderline papers whose baseline accept
probabilities lie in the $`0.45`$–$`0.50`$ range and spawn 5
section-specific agents per paper, one for each section family:
Introduction, Background / Related Work, Methodology, Experiments /
Results, and Discussion / Conclusion. The editing agent is Codex on
gpt-5.5 with medium reasoning and no web search. Each agent is
restricted to one section and is not allowed to change any numerical
results, but it may improve framing, exposition, ordering, and technical
detail within that section. Each commit the Codex agents submit is
scored by our fine-tuned PaperScorer-Text, evaluated greedily at
temperature $`0`$ with logprobs.

|  |  |
|----|----|
| Category |  Description |
| Substantiation |  Introducing concrete evidence from tables and figures into the paper text. |
| Formalization |  Formalizing notation and stating implicit equations, explicit definitions, or proof structures. |
| Narrative |  Restructuring sections to reframe motivation or alter content flow. |
| Calibration |  Ensure that sentiment matches the scope of results by adjusting overclaims, tempering language, and acknowledging weaknesses. |
| Nuance |  Clarifying ambiguous phrasing, defining terms, or improving precision of descriptions. |

Table L.2: Paper revision strategy taxonomy. We define the edit
categories used to label section-level perturbations.

### L.3 Edit Analysis

Section attention trends. As noted in the main text, the section-level
attention averages show a clear ordering that prioritizes later
sections. The example heatmap in [Figure
L.2](#A12.F2 "Figure L.2 ‣ L.2 Interpretability Details ‣ Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")
illustrates this qualitative pattern, with attention clustering tightly
around technical claims, result tables, and synthesis paragraphs, rather
than the opening overview. While previous literature suggests that
attention analysis alone may not definitively determine the importance
of input tokens, our causal edit analysis demonstrates that the increase
in acceptance likelihood follows this exact same ordering.

Perturbation protocol. For our section-level edit interventions, we
select 30 accepted papers from ICLR ’26 that specifically have low
presentation scores. This ensures the underlying content is of high
quality, isolating the impact of stylistic and structural improvements
on $`p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$.

We use Codex with gpt-5.5 under a medium reasoning setting to generate
edits ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib9)). The editing agent is restricted
to a single section per trial, with unlimited read and edit tool calls.
Crucially, the agent is explicitly forbidden from modifying any
numerical results, guaranteeing that changes are strictly limited to
framing, clarity, and style.

Once the agent is satisfied, it commits the updated text with a summary
statement. This process is repeated 3 more times using a naive agent
given the same prompt, without knowledge of the PaperScorer output.
After all commits are generated, we use PaperScorer to grade each
iteration.

Impact of edits by section. The rankings of the sections by
$`\Delta p_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ directly reflect the initial attention
distribution, with the majority of the score improvement coming from the
first edit commit. Edits to the Experiments / Results and Discussion /
Conclusion yield the largest gains (5.4–6.1%), followed by Methodology
(4.7%), and smaller improvements for the Introduction and Background
(3.9–4.2%). Because the maximum difference between final scores across
the sections differs by only 2%, we conclude that the attention
weighting reflects a consistent, albeit small, effect size regarding
which sections the model prioritizes. We also hypothesize that the
effect size is partially due to the authors’ allocation of time. The
introductions of papers are typically written quite well, as they
provide the first impression for a reviewer or reader. Therefore, there
may be fewer style changes that may improve the paper. On the other
hand, the results themselves are typically more important than the style
of reporting them, so there may be more stylistic things to update in
later sections.

Optimal edit strategies. We also examine the types of edits Codex makes
in each section and which types our model favors. Using the commit
messages, we classify each edit into specific categories (detailed in
Table
[L.2](#A12.T2 "Table L.2 ‣ L.2 Interpretability Details ‣ Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")).
As illustrated in [Figure
L.1](#A12.F1 "Figure L.1 ‣ L.1 Section-Attention Map ‣ Appendix L What is PaperScorer Looking At? ‣ PaperScorer: How Predictable Is Paper Acceptance?")b,
the success rate of these edits is highly section-dependent:

- •
  Introduction: Benefits most from adding Nuance (+11%) and Calibration
  (+5%). Adjusting the Narrative here decreases the score (-13%).
- •
  Background / Related Work: Improves most from Substantiation (+8%) and
  Narrative framing (+8%), but is penalized by added Nuance (-12%).
- •
  Methodology: Only Formalization is effective (+14%), whereas all other
  edit types negatively impact the score.
- •
  Experiments and Discussion: Narrative edits yield the highest positive
  returns in both the Experiments (+12%) and Discussion (+24%) sections.
  Crucially, attempting to introduce new Substantiation into the
  Discussion serves as the most detrimental edit overall (-29%),
  suggesting that this final section should focus on interpreting
  results rather than reiterating evidence.

These edit success distributions reflect general paper guidelines,
suggesting that our model has learned the overall structure of a paper.
````
